text:
I am writing in strong opposition to the proposal to rescind the Roadless Rule. As a property owner in California, I am an active member of both my local and state native plant society, and I stay current on the drought and fire issues spanning our state and beyond. I care deeply about protecting our remaining wild and open spaces and the critical habitat they provide. Road construction is one of the most well-documented drivers of habitat fragmentation and water degradation, disrupting wildlife corridors that sensitive species depend on.

And I know I am not alone in this viewpoint. During the original rulemaking process, the Roadless Rule drew a record volume of public comment, overwhelmingly in favor of protection. That level of public investment should not be ignored.

The stated reasoning for this proposal also goes against the agency's own research, which shows that fuels treatment and wildfire mitigation already occur in roadless areas. While road access may make this work easier, it comes with real ecological costs, including erosion and the spread of invasive species.

I urge the agency to withdraw this proposal and keep the Roadless Rule intact. There are many better paths toward wildfire resilience and sound forest management — rescinding the Roadless Rule is not one of them.

The 2001 Roadless Area Conservation Rule conserves over 58 million acres of multiple-use public lands managed by the U.S. Forest Service that provide some of the best places to hunt and fish in America. Repealing safeguards afforded by the Roadless Rule will jeopardize intact fish and wildlife habitat and I urge the U.S. Department of Agriculture to uphold strong protections for all roadless areas.   

Across the country, roadless areas provide irreplaceable habitat for native trout and salmon, big game, and other wildlife. The 2001 Roadless Rule generally prohibits new road construction and industrial logging, while at the same time keeping these public lands open to habitat improvement projects, hazardous fuels reduction, hunting, fishing, OHV riding, firewood cutting, grazing, and camping.   

The 2001 Roadless Rule already allows for balanced forest management, including timber harvest, to reduce the risk of uncharacteristic wildfire, as well as to restore habitat for sensitive fish and wildlife species. Importantly, hazardous fuels treatments in roadless areas are commonplace, helping protect at-risk communities and restoring forest health.     

If rescinded, new road construction and associated industrial-scale logging will fragment fish and wildlife habitat, degrade water quality and quantity, and reduce backcountry hunting and fishing opportunities on public lands. There are 370,000 miles of roads in the National Forest System with a maintenance backlog of $10.8 billion, 55% of which is due to dilapidated roads that cause sedimentation and erosion that reduce water quality, create barriers to fish migration, and create public safety hazards. We need to take care of the roads we already have, not add more roads that we don’t have the funding or personnel to maintain. 

Roadless areas provide some of the best fish and wildlife habitat and hunting and angling opportunities for Americans of all walks of life. I strongly support maintaining protections for all roadless areas and keeping these public lands a great place to hunt and fish.

text:
As someone who accesses roadless national forest regularly and has observed the significant differences between those areas and adjacent roaded lands, I urge the Department to reconsider a rescission whose administrative rationale does not appear proportionate to the long-term public cost of the action.

Building roads through these critical wildlands threatens to tear down the very places that make America Beautiful. These roadless places are where countless Americans go to connect with the outdoors, and in doing so contribute mightily to tourism economies around the country. Many communities have relied on tourism for the last 25 years, with the understanding that adjacent public lands would be protected for many years to come. This is a betrayal to the small towns of the West.

While exploring America's most wild and beautiful places, I have seen firsthand how these places improve people's lives. I have built connections in rural communities that rely on these places. Through these connections, I have learned that protecting these lands is not a rural vs. urban debate, or really even a political one. Americans have spoken. We value our public lands. Stripping protections will win corporate favor, but lose the trust of the people the land belongs to: all Americans.

The forest service is charged with managing these lands in a way that benefits Americans to the highest degree possible. That includes those who recreate on these pristine lands. That includes those whose livelihoods rely on the people who recreate there. If the department cannot guarantee the protection and preservation of its roadless areas, then it has fundamentally failed all future Americans, who will not see the short-term benefits of industry, but will feel the absence of places that the forest service failed to protect. Additionally, wildland fires are highly connected to human activity, and the construction of remote roads is likely to cause more fires in remote areas that are difficult to fight. The argument that new roadways will help to prevent fires is a bad-faith argument designed to justify the expansion of industry. It is a betrayal to the legacy of the Department, the brave first responders who protect us from wildfires, and to all Americans.

Rescinding the roadless rule would be a failure to follow the mission of the department, and a blatant display of unchecked corporate influence. The forest service has spent many decades building trust with voters. Today, it is poised to erase that trust in a single pen stroke. On behalf of the people of America, please do not rescind the Roadless Rule.

CommentID: RLC-20260821-SPJ7UY

text:
I have recreated in National Forests almost every near since I was 5 years old.  I am now 74.  I have been in National Forests in at least 13 states in the East, South, West, and Alaska.  I live approximately 2 miles from a National Forest and not much farther from an IRA.  I taught environmental science courses at Harvard University and Waseda University (summer 2010), as well as at the National Humanities Center in North Carolina.
Document FS-2025-0001-224067, “Proposed Rule: Special Areas; Roadless Area Conservation; National Forest System Lands, Cost Benefit Analysis and
Consideration of Impacts on Small Entities,” does not present a compelling case at all for rescinding the Roadless Rule.
Building more roads will generally  worsen forest conditions, increase the probability of wildfires, degrade water quality, likely introduce invasive flora, impinge on crucial wildlife habitat, and provide little increase in recreation opportunities aside from riding more ATVs and dirt bikes.
The proposed annual timber increased gross income ($9.9 to $22.0 million) would be wiped away—and far, far more—by the costs of fighting one significant wildfire.  The Dixie fire in California cost about $540 million to fight.  The clear majority of wildfires are human caused, and the clear majority of those start within one-third of a mile from a road.  More roads in IRAs are a good way to increase the probability of wildfires.  In the West, forest thinning often leads to lower humidity and greater wind speeds within the forest, and thus spreads wildfires faster.  No studies consistently show that forest thinning is a good way to prevent wildfires.  The best thing to do is to harden homes and other structures.  That’s where the money should be spent.  See Sen. Sheehy and Padilla’s bill, The Community Protection and Wildfire Resiliency Act, S. 3609. 
Only about 5% of US timber production comes from FS land.  There appears no strong market force that would argue to increase that production.
The General Mining Law already provides access for mineral resources and exceptions are granted where compelling circumstances are presented.  As for energy, Document FS-2025-0001-224067 states that rescinding the Roadless Rule would produce “no net change in domestic leasable production . . . because leasable mineral development in IRAs could still occur based on technological methods of extraction without the use of roads or would replace or substitute existing development outside of IRAs on federal, state, or private lands resulting in no net change in domestic production.” (p. 24).
I live in Montana, where many hunters and anglers and their associations support the current Roadless Rule.
There is already a road maintenance backlog for existing roads, which is underfunded.
Would there be benefits to rescinding the Roadless Rule?  Yes, for a few, select companies and perhaps for a few communities.  However, those benefits are non-quantifiable, cannot be projected accurately, and are far outweighed by the benefits provided by maintaining the current Roadless Rule, benefits that are human and ecological.
US National Forests cover about 190 million acres.  Please leave 45 million of those acres (less than 25%) under the Roadless Rule.

text:
Dear Secretary Rollins:

As a California native, I have watched fires become more and more common over my lifetime. As a child, smoke-filled Falls and wildfire go-bags were never a concern. Now, they are commonplace. I have also seen our progression as a country, as we have learned about wildfire and its causes. We now understand that some ecosystems, and many in the Western US, have evolved with fire as a natural process, and that a policy of fire suppression is counterproductive. The evidence shows that rescinding the Roadless Rule will only exacerbate this problem.

Suppression has degraded fire-dependent ecosystems. A century of aggressive fire suppression — made possible by road access — has transformed fire-adapted forests like longleaf and ponderosa pine. Without periodic low-intensity fire, fuels accumulate and forest structure shifts toward conditions that support catastrophic, stand-replacing fires (USDA Forest Service 2001). — USDA Forest Service, Pacific Northwest Research Station, May  (https://www.fs.usda.gov/pnw/pubs/pnw_gtr509.pdf)

Roadless areas maintain more natural fire regimes. Because roadless areas lack the access that enables intensive suppression and the traffic that brings human ignitions, they retain fire patterns closer to what their ecosystems evolved with. Adding roads changes both ends of the equation at once (Aplet et al. 2026; USDA Forest Service 2001). — Gregory H. Aplet, Phil Hartger, Matthew S. Dietz, 2026 · Fire Ecology (https://doi.org/10.1186/s42408-026-00450-2)

I have seen firsthand the devastation that fire can ravage on our communities. In 2017 I worked at a Barnes and Nobel just North of San Francisco. One of my jobs was to dust the every book and shelf because they had become blanketed with dust and debris that had settled from the smoky air generated from the Tubbs Fire. In that same fire, my friend lost her home in Santa Rosa, fleeing just in time, only able to save her pets. It is imperative that we listen to the science and make sound decisions about the management of our environment that will protect both it and ourselves.

I respectfully urge the Department to allow the Rule to stand and to decline the rescission action now proposed.


CommentID: RLC-20260901-MYMWEC

text:
USDA,

I write to urge you to please not rescind the Roadless Rule. There are millions of acres of forest that hold much more value to us than just economic. 
These lands are some of the last areas of our country where wildlife is allowed to flourish and grow. Without these forests, there will be no place for our native elk, deer, or wolves to live and thrive. Food sources would go scarce, breeding grounds would be sparse, and migration would be stalled or prevented. 
Recently (end of July 2025), lynx kittens have been found in northeastern Washington, marking the return of a keystone species to our environment. With this rule, we could be threatening an important animal to our ecosystems and subsequently throwing nature's harmony off-balance. This is only one example of the many species that could be harmed if this protection is taken away from them. 
Along with this, people all across the U.S. use these lands for hunting, fishing, recreation, and some tribes even use them for ceremonies. Proposing to rescind this rule ignores the cultural significance of these lands and the importance of them for our existing industries.
In regards to wildfires, this rule should still not be rescinded. Most wildfires start because of human activity, not because of natural phenomena. Research suggests that building more roads onto roadless areas will actually increase the chance of wildfires. 
I am again imploring you to not rescind the roadless rule, for the good of our forests, and more importantly for the good of our wildlife’s forests. 

Thank you for your time,
Maddie Adriazola

text:
Secretary Rollins:

In Central Oregon, we have almost 200,000 acres of Inventoried Roadless Areas in the Deschutes National Forest, Ochoco National Forest, and Crooked River National Grassland that have protected wildlife habitat, boosted local economies, and ensured clean drinking water for 25 years. 

From protecting recreational opportunities in Newberry Caldera, to safeguarding sweeping views atop Lookout Mountain in the Ochocos, to maintaining mule deer and elk migration corridors in the Metolius Basin, the Roadless Rule is vital to our local communities.

I STRONGLY OPPOSE THE USDA’S PROPOSAL to eliminate, alter, or weaken the Roadless Rule, which would reduce protections across 44.7 million acres of public lands managed by the US Forest Service nationwide. The agency should select Alternative 1, the No Action alternative, and leave current roadless protections in place. 

Rescinding the Roadless Rule is not practical. The USFS already has billions of dollars in deferred maintenance on its existing 370,000+ miles of roads, and this rule rescission will only compound the problem by adding expensive, infrequently used backcountry roads on the taxpayers’ dime. Worse still, in areas like Central Oregon, where the timber industry has been in decline for decades, opening roadless areas to logging will not yield a meaningful economic return. Instead, increasing roads will damage recreation areas, scenic views, and wildlife habitat, and eliminate the core reasons people choose to live, work, and play in Central Oregon.

Rescinding the Roadless Rule is also dangerous. More roads also mean more fires: research shows wildfires are four times more likely to ignite near roads. Fighting those fires in remote areas is dangerous, costly, and diverts resources from protecting communities. More roads will also degrade drinking watersheds. National Forests and Grasslands are the single most important source of municipal water supply in the United States, and Roadless Areas filter drinking water for over 2 million Oregonians. In Central Oregon, the Bend Municipal Watershed begins in the headwaters of Bridge Creek and Tumalo Creek in the Deschutes National Forest. Losing Roadless protections will threaten water quality for fish species and the drinking water supply for more than 100,000 people in Bend, and tens of millions of people across the country.

Rescinding the Roadless Rule also makes our forests less resilient. Roads spread invasive species, disrupt wildlife corridors, and erode forest resilience amid rapidly shifting wildfire regimes. Logging these roadless forests would also directly eliminate overstory and understory habitats, harm First Foods, and reduce the carbon storage we need to combat climate change.

This rescission would not, as the DEIS claims, restore our local forest managers' decision-making power. Instead, as the DEIS expressly admits, it would further the misguided goal of ramping up timber production on public lands while disempowering the Forest Service staff and Central Oregonians who care for these roadless areas.

Sacrificing our local values for short-term logging profits is not sound policy; it is a net loss for communities, economies, and future generations. Roadless forests represent some of the most intact, resilient ecosystems left in our country, but once roads and clearcuts fragment our landscapes, the damage is permanent. 

Despite the clear consequences of rescission and the vocal majority opposing the Proposed Rule, the USDA continues this rollback through an abridged and inadequate public comment process. The original Roadless Rule resulted from the most extensive public engagement process in the history of federal rulemaking, with over 95% of commenters supporting strong protections. Now, the agency is attempting to dismantle these protections with zero public meetings, shortened comment periods, and a disregard for the public input received during scoping. This is undemocratic and deeply irresponsible for decisions of such sweeping consequence.

For more than two decades, the Roadless Rule has been a cornerstone of sound forest management, balancing ecological, economic, and cultural values. Weakening or repealing it would be a grave mistake. Both Alternatives 2 and 3 will have severe consequences for wildlife, biodiversity, clean water sources, climate resilience, cultural resources, local economies, outdoor recreation, and the health of our nation's wildest forests.

The USDA should abandon this damaging effort and instead strengthen its commitment to protecting the clean water, climate resilience, recreation, and biodiversity that roadless forests provide. I urge the agency to take the No Action alternative and maintain full Roadless Rule protections for America's wild forests.

Sincerely,

Erik Horeis

text: I am writing to voice my absolute opposition to the USDA and U.S. Forest Service proposal to rescind or modify the 2001 Roadless Area Conservation Rule. This rule protects nearly 45 million acres of intact national forestland from destructive industrial logging and road building. Repealing these baseline protections is a severe step backward for conservation, wildlife, and taxpayers alike.I urge the Forest Service to reject the repeal and uphold the 'No Action' Alternative (Alternative 1) to maintain the current rule in its entirety. My opposition is based on the following critical points:Repealing the Rule Increases Wildfire Risk: The administration claims that removing restrictions will reduce wildfire risk, but scientific consensus proves the exact opposite. A 2025 analysis by the Wilderness Society shows that wildfire density is lowest in roadless, protected areas. Forest Service data confirms that the vast majority of human-caused fire ignitions occur on or near roadsides. Adding more roads will inevitably invite more human-caused blazes.Fiscal Irresponsibility: The U.S. Forest Service already manages over 370,000 miles of existing roads and suffers from a staggering $8-to-$10 billion maintenance backlog. It makes absolutely no policy or financial sense to build new roads into remote, pristine backcountry when we cannot afford to maintain the infrastructure we already have.Ecological Destruction and Habitat Fragmentation: Carving roads into intact landscapes fractures vital wildlife habitats, introduces invasive species, and causes severe soil erosion that chokes watersheds. Over a third of Americans rely on these roadless headwaters for clean, cold drinking water.Economic and Recreational Value: These lands protect over 43,000 miles of public trails used by hikers, campers, hunters, and anglers. Keeping these spaces roadless preserves local tourism and outdoor recreation economies that rely on pristine natural settings.The Draft Environmental Impact Statement fails to justify why opening a third of our National Forest System to commercial exploitation is necessary. Public sentiment is overwhelmingly clear—historic comment periods showed 95% to 99% support for maintaining these protections. I demand that the Forest Service listen to the public and the science: Do not repeal the Roadless Rule.

text:
I would like to provide comment to reject the idea of rescinding the Roadless Rule. As an avid outdoorsman, hunter, fisherman, and professional chef and occasional guide, I cannot imagine a world where increased human impact will improve these wild places. Let alone does it make sense to increase the reach of modern forest management by an administration that has gutted the current Forest Service workforce. One of the true beacons of this country is that public lands are treated as such, not invaded by contractors for resource extraction. I fail to recall a time when allowing mineral extraction and disrupting migration routes of animals has improved the landscape, but I readily can see examples of the contrary. I am highly confident that we all are aware of that fact, I just refuse to turn a blind eye to it leading to anything but exploitation, pollution, and loss of habitat. I've personally seen hundreds if not thousands of acres of wetlands absolutely destroyed by subdivision development in my state of Illinois. I have also seen great improvements over the last 2 decades as we have actively worked to restore these habitats. Midewin Tallgrass Prairie is a great example of these efforts, which is managed by the USFS and Army Corps of Engineers if I'm not mistaken. The things you can see out there since the roads have been closed off is absolutely stunning. I've seen waterways restored as we've limited human impacts of them in the Rock and Kishwaukee Rivers. I know that you all know this isn't the best thing for long term enviromental health. So I encourage you to abandon this idea of exploiting one of the few things that truly sets this country apart. Without the sharing of the land with the public and nature, we are no longer special in any way. 

Cheers,
Justin Moser

I OPPOSE the repeal of the Roadless Rule by the USDA.  I was born and raised in NH and hold the wild parts of the White Mountain National Forest (WMNF) as extremely important for my family, for the State of NH, and for the nation at large.  My family hikes regularly in the "Whites".   The Rule is important to us personally, but it also profoundly important to the nation and the natural world.

To preserve the protection of the Rule, and to voice the opposition of the people of New Hampshire, the NH House of Representatives passed House Resolution 44 in March 2026.  The Resolution explicitly urges support for keeping public ownership of public lands and OPPOSES EFFORTS TO RESCIND THE ROADLESS RULE. 

The Rule affects only 30% of the WMNF leaving 60% of the WMNF available to commercial interests.  The proportion of affected forest land is the same on the national level in that only 30% of the National Forest System is protected by the Rule.  The rule has no effect on the vast amounts of timberland privately held in NH and across the nation.  The claim that the rule impedes timber harvesting is exaggerated.  It ignores the importance protected natural lands to the welfare of our society, to the mental health of each citizen of the USA, and to the millions of tourists who affected by their grandeur.

This commentary is written in regard to the potential rescission of the Roadless Rule. While not someone who frequently writes in support of or against potential laws, this is a matter of such importance that I’m compelled to comment. For a number of reasons, the Rescission of the Roadless Rule is a very poor idea. I strongly oppose the US Dept of Agriculture’s proposal to rescind this key conservation rule and I offer reasoning in the following paragraphs.
 
First, the USFS suggests that building more roads will aid in fire management, but statistics strongly contradict this being true. Over 90% of wildfires are human caused and occur within ¼ to ½ mile of a road. Building more roads will mean MORE devastating wildfires!  I’ve seen this upclose and personal this year as the Reno area has had five large wildfires causing millions of dollars of property and environmental damage as well as loss of life…and ALL were human caused. The last thing that the dry west needs is more opportunities for devastating human caused wildfires.
 
In addition, the USFS has more than 370,000 miles of roads which it already cannot afford to maintain. Adding more roads would cause further backlogs to maintenance issues of current roads.  USFS, as with all federal land management agencies, has been underfunded for its entire existence, no matter which political party has been in office. The last thing that is needed is to further overwhelm the agency with more fiscal challenges.
 
Further, roadless areas protect clean drinking water for over 60 million Americans as well as wildlife found on USFS lands. Road construction, grading, and timber harvesting increase runoff, sedimentation, and stream degradation. 
 
Finally, roadless areas are extremely valuable for recreational opportunities and the small local communities who provide services for visitors. Pack stations are solid traditional rural businesses which cater to fisherman, hunters, and hikers/backpackers… as well as professional photographers. Small camp stores support campers who come to the area to hike, fish, hunt, or simply spend a tranquil time getting away from it all in serene wild areas.  Hotels and restaurants also are supported by outdoor enthusiasts. Once an area becomes accessible to vehicles, the intrinsic wild value is lost. For those who desire or need easy access, there are already many, many federal and state properties which offer easy access.
 
In conclusion, I reiterate that I totally oppose the rescission of the roadless rule for the reasons stated above.  
 
Sincererly,
Jaci Wollenberg
jm_wollenberg@yahoo.com

text:
As a resident of New Jersey—the most densely populated state in the country—I am writing to strongly oppose the proposed repeal of the 2001 Roadless Area Conservation Rule.
While New Jersey does not have expansive National Forest System lands within its borders, those of us living in the Mid-Atlantic deeply value and depend on the protection of our nation's remaining pristine public lands. I oppose the rescission of these protections for the following reasons:
• Climate and Watershed Protection: The 45 million acres protected by the Roadless Rule act as massive carbon sinks and safeguard critical watersheds. Climate change impacts everyone, and rolling back protections on these forests will accelerate carbon emissions and degrade water quality across state lines.
• Preserving Outdoor Recreation for All Americans: For residents of highly urbanized states like New Jersey, America's National Forests are premier destinations for travel, hiking, camping, and experiencing true wilderness. Fragmenting these lands with industrial roads and logging will permanently destroy the backcountry spaces that millions of Americans travel across the country to visit.
• Flawed Fire-Management Justification: The Forest Service's claim that repealing the rule is necessary for wildfire management contradicts its own historical data. Independent and agency studies show that building more roads does not improve forest health or create more effective fire management; instead, it often introduces new ignition sources and invasive species.
Once these wild spaces are fragmented by roads, oil and gas leasing, and commercial logging, they can never be fully restored. Please protect these shared public lands for future generations and maintain the Roadless Area Conservation Rule in its entirety.
Thank you for considering my comments.

text:
I live in Flagstaff, Arizona and am writing to urge the U.S. Department of Agriculture to retain the 2001 Roadless Area Conservation Rule and select the No Action Alternative. My connection to National Forest lands includes as a natural resource professional and research scientist with a Ph.D., as a recreationist who hikes, backpacks, runs, and camps, among other things, on public lands, and someone who lives in a community surrounded by National Forest. Roadless and undeveloped public lands provide protection for all species and ecosystem components to exist in forests that are relatively undisturbed by intensive human activities like timber harvests and roads.

Among other issues, wildlife habitat, landscape connectivity, and watershed and drinking water integrity are at risk. Roadless areas contain higher biodiversity and protect watershed integrity (Olden et al. 2026, Mildrexler et al. 2026). This protects drinking water for millions of people. Biodiversity protects all species and provides access to quality hunting and fishing valued by many. 

It is unclear how the USDA is weighing wildfire, management flexibility, and the effects of increased access. Roadless areas burn at about the same rate and severity as roaded areas and less often than designated Wilderness Areas (Kilbride et al. 2026, Johnston et al. 2021). Fire ignitions are higher along roads, which are then likely to increase if roadless areas become roaded (Aplet et al. 2026).

Before rescinding the national rule, I would like USDA to answer these questions: How would USDA ensure that roadless values are protected through individual forest plans and project-level decisions if the national rule is removed? Why aren’t the existing exceptions sufficient? How does the USDA reconcile the existing research with the justification of rescission with regard to wildfire risk? Rather than rescind the rule, careful review of the existing exceptions and implementation should be undertaken. Perhaps changes can happen to allow for faster implementation within the exceptions rather than rescinding the entire rule. 
Rescinding the rule would negatively impact my ability to participate in my preferred recreational activities in the same way, while also threatening the drinking water I rely on. It may also increase the threat of wildfire to my home and community by extending roads into currently roadless areas. 
 For these reasons, I urge the USDA to retain the 2001 Roadless Area Conservation Rule and select the No Action Alternative. Thank you for considering my comments.
Citations:
Aplet, G.H., Hartger, P. and Dietz, M.S., 2026. Three-decade record of contiguous-US national forest wildfires indicates increased density of ignitions near roads. Fire Ecology, 22(1), p.8.
Johnston, J.D., Kilbride, J.B., Meigs, G.W., Dunn, C.J. and Kennedy, R.E., 2021. Does conserving roadless wildland increase wildfire activity in western US national forests?. Environmental Research Letters, 16(8), p.084040.
Kilbride, J.B., Johnston, J.D., Kennedy, R.E., Meigs, G.W. and Francis, E.M., 2026. Roadless status under the Roadless Area Conservation Rule is not associated with increased wildfire in the US National Forest System. Conservation Science and Practice, p.e70411.
Mildrexler, D.J., Berner, L.T., Law, B.E. and Booth, M.S., 2026. Roadless rule rescission threatens highest integrity forest ecosystems in the United States. Biological Conservation, 321, p.111950.
Olden, J.D., Postel, S.L., Dombeck, M.P., Kesting, H., Freeman, P. and Comte, L., 2026. Assessing the value of the US Roadless Rule for people and nature. PLOS Water, 5(7), p.e0000538.

Dear Secretary Rollins and Chief Schultz:

The pollution becomes more deadly. The temperatures continue to rise. Animals are dying as their homes are cut down leading to potential ecosystem collapse. If they go, we go too.

As a citizen whose climate worry shapes how I vote, what I read, and now what I comment on, the 2001 Rule keeps a meaningful amount of carbon in trees. That's the version of climate action that does the math.

Regarding the Big Island in the Chippewa National Forest, Minnesota:

I want to Department to understand the long term effects and the world they are giving their kids and their kids kids. I want them to think of the future.

Intact roadless landscapes support functional soils, hydrology, and food webs that fragmented forests cannot replicate.

Most remaining forest is already fragmented. Globally, 70 percent of remaining forest is within one kilometer of a forest edge — within the zone where edge effects compromise interior conditions. The remaining intact interior, including roadless areas in the National Forest System, has become disproportionately important for sustaining the species and processes that require unfragmented forest (Haddad et al. 2015). — Haddad et al., 2015 (https://doi.org/10.1126/sciadv.1500052)

Rescinding the Roadless Rule would open the Big Island, Chippewa National Forest to road construction and associated ground disturbance. The direct and indirect effects of that activity are precisely what makes a specific comment about this area necessary.

The proposed action should be withdrawn, and the 2001 Rule allowed to remain operative.

With gratitude,

I live in portsmouth, ohio and am writing to urge the U.S. Department of Agriculture to retain the 2001 Roadless Area Conservation Rule and select the No Action Alternative. My connection to National Forest lands includes hiking and backpacking, camping, and wildlife watching. It is important to me that these lands remain undeveloped for peace and enjoyment.

I am concerned about the cost of expanding the National Forest road system. The government cannot maintain the roads that we already have, so it would be a poor decision to create more.

I am concerned about wildlife habitat and landscape connectivity. Disruption of wildlife habitats can have a destructive cascading effect on multiple species leading to potential direct harm to the local flora and fauna and could result in agricultural and fiscal harm to the humans in the local areas.

I am concerned about clean water and healthy watersheds. We, and all other creatures, need clean water to survive.  Adding roads and development to these lands WILL increase water pollution in the area and cause harm.

I am concerned about increased timber-development pressure in currently roadless areas. It is morally reprehensible to lift safeguards in order to allow logging companies to ravage protected lands for more profit.

Before rescinding the national rule, I would like USDA to answer this question: Why are the Roadless Rule's existing exceptions insufficient to meet legitimate wildfire, public safety, and forest-management needs?

For these reasons, I urge USDA to retain the 2001 Roadless Area Conservation Rule and select the No Action Alternative. Thank you for considering my comments.

text:
I oppose the proposal to fully or partially rescind the 2001 Roadless Area Conservation Rule (Docket FS-2025-0001).
Introduction & Stance
As a resident who values public lands, clean water, and intact ecosystems, I strongly urge the U.S. Forest Service and the U.S. Department of Agriculture to select Alternative 1 (the No Action alternative) and keep the 2001 Roadless Rule fully intact. Rescinding or altering these protections across tens of millions of acres of national forests would be a permanent mistake for our environment, wildlife, and municipal water supplies.
Core Reasons to Retain the Roadless Rule
• Protection of Clean Water: National forest roadless areas serve as vital source watersheds. They provide clean drinking water to over 60 million Americans across thousands of communities. Removing roadbuilding and logging bans risks severe erosion, sedimentation, and water treatment burdens.
• Wildlife Habitat & Biodiversity: Roadless areas provide unbroken, quiet corridors that support hundreds of at-risk and imperiled species. New roads fragment these pristine habitats, encouraging invasive species and disrupting migration corridors.
• Wildfire Realities: Claims that rolling back the rule will reduce wildfire risks are contradicted by science. Road corridors increase human access and activity, which account for the vast majority of human-caused wildfire ignitions. Furthermore, open canopies along roads dry out understory vegetation.
• Preserving Backcountry Recreation: The rule does not lock the public out; rather, it protects the undeveloped backcountry character that makes activities like hiking, hunting, fishing, and backcountry camping exceptional. Localized, fragmented management will only erode these baseline protections.
Conclusion
For all these reasons, I ask the agency to reject the proposed rescission and maintain the robust, nationwide protections of the 2001 Roadless Rule.

text:
I strongly oppose the proposal to fully rescind the Roadless Area Conservation Rule. I urge the U.S. Forest Service to maintain the Roadless Rule and continue protecting our nation’s remaining roadless National Forest lands.

Roadless areas are some of the last places where people can experience intact forests, clean water, wildlife habitat, and quiet recreation without the impacts associated with roads, logging, and development. These lands have value far beyond the timber that could potentially be extracted from them. Once a road is built and a previously undeveloped area is fragmented, the ecological and recreational qualities that made that land valuable in the first place can be permanently diminished.

The argument that rescinding the Roadless Rule is necessary for wildfire and fuels management is particularly concerning. Increasing road access and development does not automatically mean healthier forests or fewer catastrophic fires. The information presented in the environmental analysis indicates there is not substantive evidence that roadless areas inherently burn more than developed or roaded areas. Rescinding protections could instead increase human access and ignition risk while opening previously protected areas to additional disturbance.

I am also concerned about the cost of expanding and maintaining a road system on public lands. The Forest Service already faces significant challenges maintaining existing roads. Building additional roads creates long-term maintenance obligations, while timber revenues are not necessarily sufficient to cover those costs. I do not believe our public lands should be opened to permanent infrastructure and environmental impacts when the economic benefit does not justify the expense.

The impacts on water, soil, air quality, and biodiversity are also significant. Road construction and logging can contribute to erosion, sedimentation, nutrient runoff, and other changes to forest and aquatic ecosystems. Roadless areas provide important habitat for wildlife and threatened and endangered species and help preserve connected ecosystems. Fragmenting these areas also creates opportunities for the introduction and spread of invasive species.

There is also a substantial recreational and economic value associated with keeping these lands intact. People travel to and spend money in communities because of access to forests, wilderness-like recreation, hunting, fishing, hiking, camping, wildlife viewing, and other outdoor experiences. That economic value should be considered alongside the relatively limited revenue that could be generated through timber harvest in roadless areas. Public lands should not be evaluated solely by the amount of timber that can be removed from them.

Finally, I urge the Forest Service to carefully consider the rights, cultural resources, and interests of Tribal Nations and Indigenous communities. Road construction, logging, and increased access can affect culturally significant plants, subsistence resources, sacred sites, and habitat relied upon by Indigenous communities. Protecting roadless lands can help preserve these resources for generations.

Roadless areas are a finite public resource. Once these landscapes are fragmented by roads and development, we cannot simply restore them to their original condition. I strongly oppose fully and even partially rescinding the Roadless Area Conservation Rule and ask the Forest Service to maintain these protections for the benefit of current and future generations.

Please continue to protect the land of Indigenous nations.

text: Please protect our wild places. Rescinding the roadless rule will cause detriment to our drinking water, speed the endangerment and extinction of our wild species, and increase the chances of forest fires.  The Forest Service already has a backlog of roads that they are unable to maintain, and an insufficient budget to do so.  Most human-caused forest fires are from roads, and we already have unprecedented wildfire seasons, only getting worse with drought and climate change. Opening up these fragile areas to more human destruction has no positive effect, only negative, for us, our futures, and the future generations.  Please help preserve these wild places for our children’s children, and stop making rash decisions that continue to destroy the planet.  As a trail runner, avid hiker, and fisherwoman, I personally love and rely on these spaces for a chance to get out in nature.  I cannot be the last generation that gets to enjoy them.  Thank you for your consideration.

The roadless rule currently conserves considerable swaths of the iconic American landscape for recreation, while simultaneously protecting wildlife and irreplaceable forested lands from excessive encroachment from development. I strongly oppose this revision to the roadless rule, which pretends to be in the best interest of fire mitigation, but is truthfully an attempt to dismantle our public lands for private profit. What use is it to cut down and destroy what little woods that remain just to sell them to foreign markets that are oceans away? Further, I have not yet seen the U.S. Forest Service appropriately respond to literature supporting the roadless rule as it currently stands. I would like to see detailed review and thorough response to Kilbride et al. 2026 (DOI: 10.1111/csp2.70411), Cornwall 2026 (DOI: 10.1126/science.aem2421), Olden et al. 2026 (DOI: 10.1371/journal.pwat.0000538), and Bishop 2026 (ISSN: 0001-8368).
I believe in the strength of the USFS to protect the places Americans value most, and to serve many interests. I strongly disagree with the idea that these rule changes are in the best interest of the public, who you serve.
We are not so poor as to have to destroy our lands, nor so rich that we can afford to.

text:
Tyler Batdorf, 2221 SW 1st Ave Apt 924, Portland, OR 97201
August 20, 2026

Re: Comment in Opposition to Proposed Rescission of the 2001 Roadless Area Conservation Rule (36 CFR Part 294, Subpart B) — Docket FS-2025-0001, RIN 0596-AD66

I oppose this proposed rescission. I am a backcountry recreationist who uses inventoried roadless areas (IRAs) in Oregon and the Pacific Northwest, and I have reviewed the proposed rule and its "Summary of Potential Impacts." My comment focuses on places where the Department's own disclosures in this rule undercut its stated rationale.

**1. The wildfire rationale ignores the Forest Service's own research.** The "Rationale for the Proposal" cites wildfire risk as a reason for rescission. But the Forest Service's own Research and Development program has found that fuel-treatment activity has actually occurred at a higher per-acre rate in roadless areas than in roaded areas, and that roaded and roadless forests have burned at similar rates since 2001, a "neutrality" its researchers attribute to higher human-caused ignition near roads offsetting suppression-access gains. Recent peer-reviewed work using 30 years of national-forest fire records found ignition density roughly three times higher within 250 meters of a road than beyond 2,000 meters, and concluded new roads into roadless terrain are likely to increase total ignitions. The proposed rule does not address this research anywhere in its "Wildfire risk" discussion. I request the Department directly address its own R&D findings before finalizing this rule.

**2. The Department's own cost-benefit figures don't support the rule.** The "Summary of Potential Impacts" states rescission would open only 4.8 million acres (16%) of forested IRAs to new active management, generating just $5.2–11.4 million/year in public revenue, against a disclosed $6.9 billion road maintenance backlog, $6.1 million/year in lost recreation value, and a total annual cost the Department itself says "could exceed $100 million." I request a single reconciled accounting showing how the claimed benefits outweigh these disclosed costs, particularly given this rule's designation as "economically significant" under E.O. 12866.

**3. Case-by-case NEPA review may not reduce burden.** The rule states future projects would still require site-specific NEPA compliance at the individual forest level. Replacing one national standard with review at 175+ forest units is not self-evidently less burdensome, and the rule does not compare the administrative cost of each approach.

**4. Litigation history should factor into the durability analysis.** The rule's own "Background" section describes the 2001 Rule as having been enjoined and reinstated multiple times, including a Ninth Circuit affirmance in *California ex rel. Lockyer*. Combined with the majority Tribal opposition and consultation concerns documented in this same docket, a rushed rescission is likely to face comparable challenge, undermining the near-term benefits claimed.

**5. Thirty days is inadequate for an economically significant rule.** This comment period is shorter than the 21-day NOI period that 54 members of Congress already called insufficient, despite covering a full proposed rule, draft EIS, and cost-benefit analysis spanning ~45 million acres. I request an extension to at least 60 days.

**Conclusion:** The Department's own disclosures — not outside assumptions — show disclosed costs exceeding disclosed benefits, an unaddressed body of agency fire research cutting against the wildfire rationale, and unresolved litigation risk. I urge the Department to retain the "No Action" alternative and withdraw this proposed rescission of 36 CFR Part 294, Subpart B, or at minimum to extend the comment period and reconcile these figures before proceeding to a final rule.

Sincerely,
Tyler Batdorf

text:
I oppose full rescission. I hike, camp, and shoot on National Forest System lands, and the DEIS does not analyze how road construction forecloses those uses.

Roads are not neutral. Each corridor redraws concentrations of vehicle traffic and dispersed camping, and under 36 CFR 261.10(d) and 261.58(m) every campsite, structure, and occupied area imposes a 150-yard no-discharge buffer, plus a prohibition on firing across or on a road. One spur, especially as it pertains to extraction industries, removes far more shooting-capable ground than its physical footprint and often severs long, unobstructed lanes with competent backstops that my, and many other Americans long range marksmanship  and hunting hobbies, require (something a 25-100yd urban enclosed range cannot substitute). For example, the Croatan National Forest (just three hours away from me) banned target shooting after expanded road access, followed by commercial and private development, constricted shooting areas and interrupted countless potential safe shooting lanes, until eventually any terrain that could’ve been used as an assured backstop fell outside of areas where it was legal to shoot, with the final decision coming after a stray round managed to travel .8 miles through the forest itself and into a private residence. 


Rescission spreads that pattern across another 44.7 million acres. The DEIS reduces recreation harm to a single $6.1 million annual figure and never disaggregates dispersed shooting, despite the EXPLORE Act directive to identify target shooting opportunities. Please analyze acreage and terrain types remaining available for lawful dispersed shooting under each alternative.

The same area fragmentation degrades hiking, camping, and general living. Roads bring noise, dust, exhaust, and sediment into the air as well as headwaters serving tens of millions of Americans. Additionally, headlights and operational lighting are brought that much deeper into places whose recreational and natural value is partially derived from substantial natural darkness and quiet. Aside from people, new roads fragment habitat for bear, elk, and native trout; roughly 25% of federally listed animal species have habitat in roadless areas.

Lastly, the wildfire rationale is unsupported. About 90% of wildfires are human-caused, and human ignitions are roughly four times likelier near roads than in roadless country. USDA concedes 11.3 million roadless acres already sit near existing roads and remain untreated. Access is not a constraint; workforce capacity and a $6.9 billion road maintenance backlog are.

I urge selection of the no-action alternative.

text:
Re: Rescission of the Roadless Area Conservation Rule, Docket FS-2025-0001

This land is your land, this land is my land, from California to the New York Island! We cannot, and we should not, auction it off. That conviction drives this comment opposing the proposed rescission of the 2001 Roadless Area Conservation Rule, Docket FS-2025-0001.

California holds 381 inventoried roadless areas totaling 4,389,760 acres, and 1,034 municipal water intakes in the Pacific Southwest region sit in watersheds containing affected roadless areas. The communities drinking from those watersheds depend on the protection the 2001 rule provides. The proposal justifies rescission in part on wildfire and fuels management grounds, but the agency's own record states: "Building a road into a forest at high risk from uncharacteristic wildfire effects could increase the incidence of human-caused fires. A human-caused wildland fire is nearly five times more likely to occur on essentially roaded lands than on essentially unroaded lands." Opening these California acres to road construction does not reduce fire risk; the agency's own findings say it compounds it. I ask that the agency explain why the proposal departs from those findings and reconcile the rescission with the ignition data in its own draft environmental impact statement, DEIS Table 21, which reports far higher fire density on roaded land than inside the affected roadless areas.

The economic case for rescission is equally hard to square with the agency's record. The agency's own analysis acknowledges: "the total timber volume affected by this rule is less than 0.5 percent of total United States production, and the total oil and gas production from all National Forest System lands is currently about 0.4 percent of the current national production." The record projects $5.2 to $11.4 million a year in timber revenue to the Forest Service against recreation losses of at least $6.1 million a year, a net present value spanning -$92 million to +$199 million, and a road maintenance backlog already standing at $6.9 billion. The agency's own Cost Benefit Analysis cannot establish a net benefit. It must reconcile those numbers with the proposal before this comment period closes.

The proposal argues that state-specific approaches can adequately replace the national rule. That argument has a record. The prior attempt to substitute a state-by-state framework for the 2001 rule was litigated, and it did not survive. The agency's own materials note its expressed dissatisfaction with a nationwide approach, but the Ninth Circuit found deficiencies in the local alternative that followed. The agency must address its own prior finding that local decision-making can incrementally erode nationally significant roadless values, and explain concretely how this proposal avoids repeating those same deficiencies.

Finally, the proposal suggests the 2001 rule exceeded the agency's statutory authority. The reviewing court said otherwise: "Exercising jurisdiction pursuant to 28 U.S.C. § 1291, we REVERSE the district court’s order granting Plaintiffs declaratory relief and issuing a permanent injunction, and REMAND the case for the district court to vacate the permanent injunction." The Tenth Circuit held that the 2001 rule fell within the authority Congress granted under the Organic Act and the Multiple-Use Sustained-Yield Act and did not create de facto wilderness. If the agency now holds a contrary position, it owes the public a full explanation of its legal basis, stated plainly in this record.

Public land belongs to everyone. The 2001 Roadless Area Conservation Rule protects what cannot be replaced. I urge the agency to withdraw this proposal.

Sincerely,
Andrew Grigg

text:
To the U.S. Department of Agriculture and U.S. Forest Service:

I am writing to strongly oppose the proposed rescission of the 2001 Roadless Area Conservation Rule, published on August 20, 2026. I respectfully urge the Forest Service to withdraw this proposal and retain the protections for Inventoried Roadless Areas (IRAs) under 36 CFR Part 294, Subpart B.

The Roadless Rule protects approximately 58.5 million acres of relatively undeveloped National Forest System lands. These areas provide clean water, wildlife habitat, carbon storage, recreation, solitude, and ecological connectivity. They are among the last remaining large landscapes where natural ecosystems can function with relatively little human disturbance.

Removing these protections would make it easier for roads, logging, and other development to enter areas that have remained intact. The Forest Service estimates that rescission could affect approximately 18.2 million acres where existing forest plans could allow permanent roads and approximately 4.8 million acres of forested IRA lands where opportunities for active forest management could expand.

Road construction is not a minor change to a forest. Roads disturb soil, increase erosion and sedimentation, alter drainage, fragment wildlife habitat, increase human access, and can lead to additional development. Once an intact landscape is fragmented, the ecological damage cannot simply be reversed when a road or logging operation is eventually abandoned.

Clean water should be one of our highest priorities. Roadless forests protect watersheds and provide important benefits to communities, wildlife, agriculture, recreation, and future generations. These public benefits should not be sacrificed for short-term opportunities to extract timber or other resources.

I recognize the Forest Service's concerns about wildfire and hazardous fuels. However, wildfire management does not require eliminating nationwide roadless protections. Targeted, science-based treatments and existing exceptions can address legitimate public-safety needs without opening millions of acres to broader development.

I am also concerned that future project-level review under the National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA) cannot fully replace the protection provided by the Roadless Rule. Individual projects may appear manageable when considered separately, while the cumulative effects of roads, logging, habitat fragmentation, and increased access can permanently change an entire landscape. The Forest Service should fully consider these cumulative and indirect effects before removing the national protection.

Our national forests should not be valued solely for timber, minerals, revenue, or other commodities. Public lands belong to all Americans. Some places are valuable precisely because they remain undeveloped.

These landscapes also have cultural and spiritual importance. The proposed rule acknowledges concerns from Tribal governments regarding Tribal sovereignty, sacred sites, cultural resources, traditional gathering areas, water quality, subsistence, and ancestral lands. These concerns deserve meaningful consideration. For many people, forests, mountains, rivers, and wilderness areas are places of profound cultural, spiritual, and personal significance that cannot be assigned a monetary value.

We inherited these lands from previous generations, and we have a responsibility to pass them on intact. Economic benefits from resource extraction may be temporary, but the loss of an ancient forest, clean watershed, wildlife habitat, or culturally significant landscape can be permanent.

For these reasons, I respectfully request that the Forest Service:

Withdraw the proposed rescission of the 2001 Roadless Area Conservation Rule.
Retain 36 CFR Part 294, Subpart B and its protections for Inventoried Roadless Areas.
Select the No Action Alternative in the environmental review.
Fully evaluate cumulative and long-term impacts to water, wildlife, habitat connectivity, soil, climate resilience, recreation, and cultural resources.
Give meaningful consideration to Tribal concerns regarding sacred and culturally significant lands.
Our national forests are a national inheritance, not simply a source of profit. Some places should remain wild because their greatest value is in being preserved. Future generations deserve the opportunity to experience these forests, watersheds, and landscapes as we inherited them—not merely hear about what was lost.
I respectfully urge the Forest Service to reject the proposed rescission and retain the 2001 Roadless Area Conservation Rule.

Thank you for considering my comments and including them in the administrative record for RIN 0596-AD66, FS-2025-0001.

Respectfully

text:
Re: Rescission of the Roadless Area Conservation Rule, Docket FS-2025-0001

To what avail are the forty freedoms without a blank spot on the map? I am reminded of these words of Aldo Leopold as I have hunted, fished, and rambled in roadless areas my whole life. The Roadless Area Conservation Rule is one that helps make America great! Its rescission would erase something that cannot be rebuilt, and I oppose it without reservation.

The agency's own science dismantles the wildfire rationale offered for this proposal. The record states: "Building a road into a forest at high risk from uncharacteristic wildfire effects could increase the incidence of human-caused fires. A human-caused wildland fire is nearly five times more likely to occur on essentially roaded lands than on essentially unroaded lands." The agency has not explained how opening these areas to roads reduces fire risk when its own findings point in the opposite direction. I ask that the agency explain why this proposal departs from those prior findings and reconcile the rescission with the ignition data in its own draft environmental impact statement, which reports far higher fire density on roaded land than inside the affected roadless areas.

The economics do not support rescission either. The record acknowledges that "the total timber volume affected by this rule is less than 0.5 percent of total United States production, and the total oil and gas production from all National Forest System lands is currently about 0.4 percent of the current national production." Against that modest ceiling, the agency's own cost-benefit analysis projects $5.2 to $11.4 million a year in timber revenue to the Forest Service against recreation losses of at least $6.1 million a year, with a net present value spanning -$92 million to +$199 million, a range so wide it cannot establish a net benefit. The agency also proposes to expand a road system already carrying a $6.9 billion maintenance backlog. How does the agency justify that expansion when its own numbers cannot show the action pays?

The state-by-state rationale has already failed in court. The agency previously described its own dissatisfaction with the Roadless Rule's approach, but the move away from a national rule that followed that dissatisfaction was reviewed by the Ninth Circuit and did not survive. The agency has not addressed its own prior finding that local decision-making can incrementally erode nationally significant roadless values, nor has it explained how this proposal avoids the same deficiencies the Ninth Circuit identified the last time the agency substituted state-by-state management for a uniform national rule. The agency must answer that question directly before proceeding.

On the question of statutory authority, the Tenth Circuit has already spoken. Reviewing whether the 2001 rule exceeded the agency's power, that court held: "Exercising jurisdiction pursuant to 28 U.S.C. § 1291, we REVERSE the district court’s order granting Plaintiffs declaratory relief and issuing a permanent injunction, and REMAND the case for the district court to vacate the permanent injunction." The court found the rule within the authority Congress granted under the Organic Act and the Multiple-Use Sustained-Yield Act and did not accept the argument that the rule created de facto wilderness. The agency must state plainly, on the record, the legal basis for any position that contradicts that holding.

The animals I hunt depend on country that roads would fragment. The blank spots on the map are what make hunting and fishing worth doing. Leopold's question was not rhetorical, and neither is mine: if the forty freedoms mean anything, they require places where the land remains whole. I urge the agency to withdraw this proposal.

Sincerely,
Mike Kromrey
Springfield, Missouri

text:
Re: Rescission of the Roadless Area Conservation Rule, Docket FS-2025-0001

The Tellico and Hiawassee Rivers run clear because they begin in roadless watersheds. I paddle both rivers, and that clarity is not incidental. It is the direct product of keeping roads out of the headwaters. I have camped, hiked, and paddled in these roadless areas of the Cherokee and Nantahala National Forests for over 40 years. I am visiting the upper part of Joyce Kilmer this fall. I am writing because the Forest Service proposes to rescind the protection that makes these places what they are, and the agency's own numbers do not support doing it.

The economic case for rescission collapses when you read the agency's own record. The DEIS states that "the total timber volume affected by this rule is less than 0.5 percent of total United States production, and the total oil and gas production from all National Forest System lands is currently about 0.4 percent of the current national production." A rule affecting fractions that small does not justify dismantling protections that took decades to build. I ask the agency to reconcile the proposal with its own Cost Benefit Analysis, which projects $5.2 to $11.4 million a year in timber revenue to the Forest Service against recreation losses of at least $6.1 million a year and a net present value spanning negative $92 million to positive $199 million, and to explain how an action whose own analysis cannot establish a net benefit justifies expanding a road system already carrying a $6.9 billion maintenance backlog.

The agency also has not shown that the rule prevents anything it actually needs to do. The rule "generally banned road building subject to limited exceptions including: the preservation of 'reserved or outstanding rights' or discretionary Forest Service construction necessary for public health and safety. 36 C.F.R. Section 294.12(b)(1),(3)." The agency should identify which specific burdens are not already addressed by those exceptions, name them by category, and quantify them. That identification belongs in the record before any rescission is finalized.

I guide backpacking trips into these areas and take adults out to view what lives here. The Cheoah Bald roadless area in the Nantahala is a high-elevation resting place for hundreds of thousands of migrant birds, including some of our most threatened species. The DEIS cites findings that bird richness declines with road presence in forested habitat, and that road-noise experiments in a roadless area cut bird abundance by over a quarter, with 31 percent of species avoiding the noise entirely. With the severe decline in bird populations already underway, these undisturbed areas are not a luxury. They are a requirement for survival of the species that depend on them.  I want the agency to explain what specific mitigation would prevent the population-level harm its own cited research describes.

The Snowbird area in the Nantahala supports a large population of bears, deer, and grouse, and it does so because the lack of roads keeps it remote. The DEIS quotes the federal grizzly recovery plan: "the increased contact and conflict that come with open roads in grizzly habitat can ultimately end in grizzly mortality, and shooting, habituation and food reward all increase with the use of even secondary unpaved roads." The principle applies across bear habitat generally, and the Cherokee National Forest's verified species list includes black bear. 

Wildfire in eastern roadless areas is mostly human caused. More access means more ignition sources in ecosystems that have not been conditioned to recover from that frequency of fire. The agency has not addressed either of these feedback loops in its justification for rescission.

Finally, the proposal itself solicits "any reliance interests in the current rule that could be affected by this proposal" (91 FR 53830-31), and the Cost Benefit Analysis weighs none. I have structured over 40 years of use, guiding, and planning around the expectation that these areas remain roadless. Joyce Kilmer is one of the few places where old-growth eastern deciduous forest can still be experienced. The Cherokee holds 18 inventoried roadless areas totaling 84,881 acres. That is the landscape my reliance is built on. The agency must identify and weigh the reliance interests described in the comments it receives, including this one, before it takes any final action.

Sincerely
Wilfred M Post
Powell TN 37949

text:
Re: Rescission of the Roadless Area Conservation Rule, Docket FS-2025-0001

Hunting is a generational tradition in my family. Having truly wild areas where we can exercise our right to provide for our family matters deeply to us, and having areas where animals can be unbothered is important for population growth. The Copper Mountains roadless area in Humboldt-Toiyabe National Forest, 31,945 acres of it, has become a significant place to my family. Losing the wildness of that area by allowing roads to be introduced puts it at risk. I oppose the rescission of the 2001 Roadless Area Conservation Rule under Docket FS-2025-0001, and I ask the agency to respond to the following concerns.

The agency's own record states: "The DEIS cites the finding that elk survival rates increased during a road closure and decreased when the gates were removed (Cole 1997), and that elk avoid roads and select unroaded habitat.". It goes directly to what my family depends on in the Copper Mountains and in the other roadless areas of the Humboldt-Toiyabe. No population-level effect on big game is projected anywhere in the rescission document. The agency must project what this proposal does to big game populations and hunter opportunity, and provide that projection in the record before any final decision is made.

I have fished Lake Mead for many many years, and I have watched what happens when human activity increases. The shorelines get filthier and illegal roads increase, and that is a National Recreation Area with rangers constantly patrolling. The areas that would lose roadless protection are not patrolled that way. Opening protected areas would lead to increased pollution from vehicle emissions. Across the Intermountain region, which includes Nevada, 1,466 municipal water intakes sit in watersheds containing affected roadless areas. The drinking water crisis has been an issue my entire life here in southern Nevada, and the agency's own analysis says roads and their facilities can produce up to 90 percent of the sediment from a timber sale. The agency must explain what protections replace the rule's watershed safeguards and how sediment loading at those 1,466 intakes is addressed in the record.

The proposal claims that state-specific approaches can substitute for a national rule. The record itself states: "the USDA discussed its dissatisfaction with the Roadless Rule and highlighted its rejection of the Roadless Rule's 'inflexible "one-size-fits-all" nationwide rulemaking approach.' 70 Fed.Reg. at 25,656." That argument has been made before and the courts rejected it. I ask the agency to address its own prior finding that local decision-making can incrementally reduce nationally significant roadless values, and to explain how this proposal avoids the deficiencies the Ninth Circuit identified the last time the agency replaced the national rule with a state-by-state approach.

The agency also argues the rule imposes permitting and administrative burdens. But the rule's text shows: "It generally banned road building subject to limited exceptions including: the preservation of 'reserved or outstanding rights' or discretionary Forest Service construction necessary for public health and safety. 36 C.F.R. Section 294.12(b)(1),(3)." The burden argument requires the agency to identify which specific burdens are not already addressed by these existing exceptions, including those for public health and safety and community wildfire protection, and to quantify those burdens in the record rather than assert them in general terms.

On wildfire, the proposal uses fuels management as a justification for rescission. The agency's own record states: "Building a road into a forest at high risk from uncharacteristic wildfire effects could increase the incidence of human-caused fires. A human-caused wildland fire is nearly five times more likely to occur on essentially roaded lands than on essentially unroaded lands." That sentence belongs to the agency, not to opponents of the proposal. The La Madre - Prospect area, 278 acres in the Humboldt-Toiyabe, and Mt. Charleston, where Charleston - Macks Cyn covers 11,378 acres, are forested refuges in the Nevada heat. They are already under pressure from visitation. Adding roads increases ignition risk by the agency's own measure. The agency must explain in the record why it departs from its own prior findings on fire occurrence.

It is one thing to open a managed area to the public, but these are wild lands. Without protection, environments suffer from people who are not educated in outdoor recreation. The Currant - Duckwater B and Currant - East Slope areas have been family camping spots for decades, and implementing roads would cause them to lose their wildness. Enjoying nature has been passed through my family for generations. Being able to share these places with my children is important to me, and just like many other traditions, it deserves to be preserved.

Sincerely,
Alexis Shaul
Las Vegas, Nevada

text:
Re: Rescission of the Roadless Area Conservation Rule, Docket FS-2025-0001

I am filing this comment to oppose the proposed rescission of the 2001 Roadless Area Conservation Rule (Docket FS-2025-0001).

The scenery and the challenge of being away from civilization are what pull me into the backcountry of Washington, the eastern Sierra, and Utah, to name a few places. Since I moved to Washington in 2009 I have been visiting the Okanogan Wenatchee National Forest,  and I am continuously amazed the beauty and at all the nooks and crannies still left to explore. It would be a shame to lose them to mining and logging interests. The same holds for the inventoried roadless areas of the Mt. Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest, Gifford Pinchot National Forest, and Olympic 
National Forests, including Glacier Peak, Noisy-Diobsudand Alpine Lakes, Stephen Mather, Dan Evans, Hank Jackson, Pasayten, and Mt Baker Wildernesses.

Washington holds 139 inventoried roadless areas totaling 2,014,832 acres. These are the landscapes where I look for bears, marmots, wolverines, fishers, martens, and pika. The agency's own record gives me reason for concern about all of them. The DEIS cites findings that habitat fragmentation reduces biodiversity by 13 to 75 percent, that marten disappear when forest cover thins, and that wolverine avoid roads used by winter machines. On wider-ranging mammals, the DEIS describes how species like the grizzly bear "have suffered habitat loss and the extirpation or fragmentation of their populations." The increased contact and conflict that come with open roads in grizzly habitat can, as quoted in the DEIS, ultimately end in grizzly mortality. I ask that the agency address on the record how rescission of the rule protects the populations of wide-ranging and road-sensitive species in Washington's affected roadless areas and beyond, given its own analysis.

Re:  birds, the record speaks clearly enough. The DEIS cites findings that bird richness declines with road presence in forested habitat, and road-noise cuts bird abundance by over a quarter, with 31 percent of species avoiding the noise entirely. What does the agency propose to address those findings if it opens these areas?

The proposal justifies rescission partly on wildfire and fuels management grounds. The agency's own record states: "Building a road into a forest at high risk from uncharacteristic wildfire effects could increase the incidence of human-caused fires. A human-caused wildland fire is nearly five times more likely to occur on essentially roaded lands than on essentially unroaded lands." DEIS Table 21 reports far higher fire density on roaded land than inside the affected roadless areas. The agency must explain why the proposal departs from these findings and reconcile the rescission with the ignition data in its own environmental analysis.

The economic case for rescission is, by the agency's own accounting, thin. The DEIS records that "the total timber volume affected by this rule is less than 0.5 percent of total United States production, and the total oil and gas production from all National Forest System lands is currently about 0.4 percent of the current national production." The agency's Cost Benefit Analysis projects $5.2 to $11.4 million a year in timber revenue to the Forest Service, set against recreation losses of at least $6.1 million a year, and a net present value ranging from -$92 million to +$199 million. The road system already carries a $6.9 billion maintenance backlog. The agency must explain on the record how expanding a deficit-carrying road system is justified by numbers this uncertain.

On administrative burden: the rule the agency proposes to rescind already contains its own release valves. It "generally banned road building subject to limited exceptions including: the preservation of 'reserved or outstanding rights' or discretionary Forest Service construction necessary for public health and safety. 36 C.F.R. Section 294.12(b)(1),(3)." Exceptions also exist for existing mineral leases and community wildfire protection. The agency has not identified which specific burdens fall outside these provisions. It should do so, with numbers, before proceeding.

Finally, the proposed rule certifies no significant impact on small entities while the DEIS names outfitters, guides and tour operators as affected and its own Cost Benefit Analysis books lost recreation benefit at a minimum of $6.1 million a year. That certification is reached by spreading estimated losses across every small firm in the sector nationally rather than examining the guides and outfitters actually holding permits in affected areas, and the analysis concedes some firms may lose these receipts. The agency should withdraw the certification and conduct a proper assessment of the small entities operating in the places this rule would affect, not a national average that obscures the local harm.

Sincerely,
Megan Snyder
Seattle, WA

text:
I am writing to express my strong opposition to the U.S. Department of Agriculture and Forest Service’s proposal to fully rescind the 2001 Roadless Area Conservation Rule. Eliminating federal protections across nearly 58.5 million acres of National Forest System land—including 62,000 acres in Minnesota’s Superior National Forest—is a short-sighted decision that threatens water quality, wildlife habitat, and taxpayer dollars.

The 2001 Roadless Rule has successfully protected our wild public lands for 25 years while allowing responsible forest management, wildfire prevention, and public recreation. Rescinding this rule in its entirety is unnecessary and harmful for the following key reasons:

Threats to Water Quality and Watersheds: In Minnesota, the 62,000 acres of protected roadless area share a direct watershed with the world-renowned Boundary Waters Canoe Area Wilderness. Undeveloped forests act as natural filtration systems. Opening these areas to road building and industrial extraction endangers pristine water bodies that millions of visitors and local communities rely on for clean drinking water. My family and I personally love the Boundary Waters, spend time there every year, and rely on these wilderness areas for our mental and physical health.

Habitat Fragmentation: Fragmenting contiguous forests destroys critical habitat for vulnerable species, such as the Canada lynx. Roads cut through core hunting and denning grounds, introducing human disturbance and invasive species into areas where wild character cannot easily be recovered once lost.

Increased Wildfire Risk: While the agency cites wildfire risk reduction as a rationale for rescission, studies consistently show that nearly 90% of wildland fires originate near road access points. Expanding road networks into remote roadless areas actually increases the risk of human-caused ignitions, undermining the stated goal of community protection.

Fiscal irresponsibility: The Forest Service currently faces a multi-billion-dollar backlog in deferred road maintenance. Building expensive new roads into steep, remote terrain shifts financial burdens onto taxpayers for infrastructure the agency cannot afford to maintain, rather than prioritizing the upkeep of existing forest roads.

Public Consensus: The 2001 Roadless Rule was established after one of the most comprehensive public involvement processes in federal administrative history, supported by millions of Americans. Erasing these protections ignores a quarter-century of public advocacy and environmental stewardship.

I urge the Forest Service to withdraw the proposed full rescission of 36 CFR part 294, subpart B. Keep the 2001 Roadless Rule intact to preserve our water, wildlife, and wild public lands for generations to come.
