text:
Re: Rescission of the Roadless Area Conservation Rule, Docket FS-2025-0001

Chichagof Island stopped me cold. We spent multiple days in the Tongass National Forest, kayaking, bushwhacking, hiking through country where the wildlife and plant life are unlike anything I had words for before I got there. The scenery and wildlife were something you would only dream of seeing in your life. I can't even fathom the idea of wanting to develop this special land. The only way I can imagine someone wanting to take any protections away from this forest would be people who've never experienced its beauty. It changed me. I oppose rescission of the 2001 Roadless Area Conservation Rule and ask that this comment be entered in Docket FS-2025-0001.

The Tongass is the largest intact temperate rainforest left on Earth. It holds 110 inventoried roadless areas totaling 9,339,575 acres, with over 12,930 miles of salmon-producing streams, and roughly 44 percent of all the carbon stored by all U.S. national forests. The Tongass roadless areas I visited or named include Tenakee Ridge, Point Augusta, Trap Bay, Freshwater Bay, Whitestone, and Pavlof-East Point, places that together provide habitat for Sitka black-tailed deer, brown bear, the Alexander Archipelago wolf, bald eagle, five species of Pacific salmon, and marbled murrelet. Executive Order 14153 directs the agency to expressly exclude the Tongass from the 2001 Roadless Rule, and the Federal Register rescission notice says so in writing. Under both action alternatives, the Tongass keeps zero acres of roadless protection. That outcome is what I am asking this agency to justify.

I also hike in any national forest that allows it, and I ride trails locally while hoping for the chance to ride in national forests. The roadless areas in or near my state, among them the Clarion River, Minister Valley, Canaan Loop, Hearts Content, Dry Fork, and Glady Fork in the Allegheny and Monongahela National Forests of Pennsylvania and West Virginia, are places I want to explore the way they are meant to be seen. The Monongahela's 20 inventoried roadless areas total 174,885 acres and protect headwaters that feed the Potomac. I want to be able to reach that country on my own terms, not on a logging road. The agency should explain in its final decision how rescission serves hikers and riders whose access depends on these landscapes remaining intact.

The agency's own record makes the fire rationale for this proposal impossible to follow. It states: "Building a road into a forest at high risk from uncharacteristic wildfire effects could increase the incidence of human-caused fires. A human-caused wildland fire is nearly five times more likely to occur on essentially roaded lands than on essentially unroaded lands." If that is the agency's own finding, the proposal's reliance on wildfire management as a justification for road construction runs directly against it. I ask that the agency reconcile the rescission with the ignition data in its own draft environmental impact statement, which reports far higher fire density on roaded land than inside the affected roadless areas, and explain why the proposal departs from those prior findings.

The economic case presented for rescission is similarly difficult to accept. I want my money spent to protect these forests, not ruin them. 

Clean water matters because everyone should have the right to it, including the wildlife that depends on it. Clean water makes the world go around. More than 7,000 municipal water intakes sit in watersheds fed by these roadless areas, and the agency's own analysis indicates roads and their facilities can produce up to 90 percent of the sediment from a timber sale. Nine municipal watersheds in the Tongass are named in the DEIS, including Ketchikan, Sitka, Juneau, and Wrangell. These are not abstractions. The agency should state plainly how it intends to protect water quality in these watersheds after rescission, and what standard of review it applied to that question.

This is protected land. It serves as an important ecosystem for wildlife. It should be conserved. It should be managed responsibly, kept green, and not opened to sale or development. I ask that the agency answer each of the concerns raised here before it takes any final action.

text:
I live in Henderson, Nevada, and I spend a lot of my time hiking and camping across the Humboldt-Toiyabe National Forest and the national forests of southern Utah. I'm writing to oppose rescinding 36 CFR 294 Subpart B, in full or in part. After reading the proposed rule, I don't think the agency's own analysis supports it.

1. Local plans aren't a substitute: The rule leans on land management plans to protect roadless values. But it also confirms that forest supervisors and regional foresters can amend those plans at their discretion, and that later amendments could open up more logging and road building than what was analyzed. Leaving those foreseeable impacts out of scope understates what rescission would actually do.

2. The agency even admits the benefits are small! The rule itself calls the gains "modest and localized." Best-case timber revenue is $5.2–11.4 million a year, and that assumes harvest in every operable area, which the agency says is unlikely. Meanwhile, there's already a $6.9 billion road and bridge maintenance backlog and an estimated $6.1 million a year in lost recreation value. Giving up permanent protection on roughly 45 million acres for a return that small doesn't make sense to me???

3. The wildfire fix doesn't match the problem: Only 24% of the affected roadless acreage overlaps the wildland-urban interface, yet the proposal removes protection from all of it. The agency also concedes that more access can mean more human-caused fires. If protecting communities is the goal, an alternative focused on the wildland-urban interface would do that. Wholesale rescission goes well beyond it.

4. This affects how I use these lands: The agency acknowledges that rescission trades away "quiet, remote and self-reliant recreation." That's exactly why I go out there! Along with millions of others. The $6.1 million estimate only counts operable areas and misses what intact backcountry means to hikers, campers, and the small towns that depend on us.

5. Water and Wildlife: Roadless areas protect headwaters and habitat for native fish and wildlife. Once roads go in, the sedimentation and fragmentation are essentially permanent. Plan-level protections, on the other hand, can change with the next amendment.

6. WHO ACTUALLY BENEFITS?: This is being sold as fire policy, but the Purpose and Need section cites executive orders on expanding timber production and "unleashing" energy. The Minerals section admits new oil, gas, and coal development in roadless areas is reasonably foreseeable. Then the same section projects no net change in domestic production, and the Energy Effects section says this isn't a significant energy action. Both can't be true. If there's no real energy gain, we're giving up protected land for nothing. If there is, the analysis is wrong. 

Either way, it looks like a Trojan horse: a regulatory back door for private extractive interests into forests the public has asked, again and again, to keep intact.

7. The People have already spoken! This drew more than 220,000 letters on behalf of over 625,000 people and organizations, all who overwhelmingly opposed. The rule itself notes that most Tribal governments consulted oppose rescission too!

The record doesn't support Alternatives 2 or 3. I urge the Forest Service to adopt Alternative 1 and keep the Roadless Rule in place.

Logan Brown
Henderson, NV

text:
I am writing to comment on the proposed rule regarding Special Areas Roadless Area Conservation. I am commenting on the proposal to remove and reserve 36 CFR Part 294 Subpart B where you would rescind the 2001 Roadless Area Conservation Rules. I disagree with removing this part of the rule because the current rule limits road construction and removing trees in the roadless areas of national forests. I think there should still be protections for roadless areas, however removing this rule would allow forests to manage their own land. I disagree with the rule since building roads ruins wildlife and natural resources and even if you attempt to restore it, it will never be the same. Wildlife and resources within the forest are crucial to the community and these should be considered before removing the protections that are currently in place for the area. 
We should not rescind the rule but instead Forest Services can simply update the rule while of course still maintain protections for roadless areas. The update can allow forests the freedom to do as they wish with the area while meeting certain regulations. I think some constructions that can be allowed are the ones that have important reasons behind it such as public safety or to prevent wild fires in the forest. These are the reasons why I do not support fully removing 36 CFR Part 294, Subpart B. I think potentially updating the rules could be a better resolution since there is a way to meet both safety and protecting roadless areas.

text:
Rescission of the Roadless Area Conservation Rule, Docket FS-2025-0001

The roadless forests of Washington state, including the stretches I named in the Olympic National Forest, the Gifford Pinchot, the Wenatchee, and the Mt. Baker-Snoqualmie, are the reason I am filing this comment against the proposed rescission of the 2001 Roadless Area Conservation Rule under Docket FS-2025-0001. Washington holds 139 inventoried roadless areas totaling 2,014,832 acres. The areas I listed, among them the 86,000-acre Olympic block, the 74,650-acre Chelan unit in the Wenatchee, and the combined Mt. Baker-Snoqualmie areas running from the 6,335-acre Wobbly unit to the 415,000-acre broader forest inventory, represent exactly what the 2001 rule was written to protect. I oppose the rescission in full.

The agency frames this proposal partly as a wildfire and fuels management measure, implying that opening roadless areas to road construction will reduce fire risk. The agency's own record says the opposite. Its prior analysis states: "Building a road into a forest at high risk from uncharacteristic wildfire effects could increase the incidence of human-caused fires. A human-caused wildland fire is nearly five times more likely to occur on essentially roaded lands than on essentially unroaded lands." The roadless blocks in the Mt. Baker-Snoqualmie, including the Glacier Peak K unit at 47,269 acres, the Glacier Peak L unit at 14,084 acres, and the Glacier Peak B unit at 19,328 acres, sit in landscapes where that ignition differential is directly relevant. The agency must explain, with reference to DEIS Table 21, why this proposal departs from its own prior finding that road access raises rather than lowers human ignition rates, and must reconcile that departure with the ignition density data already in its own environmental record.

The proposal also rests on timber and energy economics. The agency's own record states: "the total timber volume affected by this rule is less than 0.5 percent of total United States production, and the total oil and gas production from all National Forest System lands is currently about 0.4 percent of the current national production." Against that baseline, the agency's own Cost Benefit Analysis projects $5.2 to $11.4 million a year in timber revenue to the Forest Service, offset by recreation losses of at least $6.1 million a year and a net present value ranging from -$92 million to +$199 million, a span so wide it cannot establish a net benefit. The Forest Service road system already carries a $6.9 billion maintenance backlog. The units I named, including the 25,390-acre Mt. Baker West and the 24,847-acre Mt. Baker Ma, sit within a forest system that cannot maintain what it already has. How does the agency justify expanding that system when its own analysis cannot demonstrate the action produces a net economic gain?

On the question of permitting and administrative burden, the agency contends the rule imposes constraints that prevent necessary management. But the rule as written already accommodates that management. The agency's own summary states it "generally banned road building subject to limited exceptions including: the preservation of 'reserved or outstanding rights' or discretionary Forest Service construction necessary for public health and safety. 36 C.F.R. Section 294.12(b)(1),(3)." The 8,676-acre Tumwater unit and the 6,570-acre Mt. Baker South unit are the kind of areas the existing exceptions were written to address. The agency must identify, with specificity, which management needs fall outside those existing exceptions, including those covering public health and safety, existing mineral leases, and community wildfire protection, and must quantify those burdens in the record rather than assert them.

Finally, the alternatives analysis underlying this proposal is built on a purpose statement written as deregulation, which eliminated every protective option before comparison could occur. The agency dismissed alternatives with more protection as not responsive to the deregulatory executive orders, and eliminated the keep-boundaries option because it "would continue to restrict local decision-making discretion" and because analysing roadless values is "an administrative and legal burden for the agency." A purpose and need framed entirely around reducing regulatory requirements cannot satisfy NEPA's requirement to consider a genuine range of alternatives. Across the Pacific Northwest region, 1,522 municipal water intakes sit in watersheds containing affected roadless areas. Rescinding the rule without honestly analysing a protective alternative treats that water supply, and every other roadless value, as outside the scope of review by design. The agency must restate the purpose and need in terms of actual forest and watershed conditions and carry at least one protective alternative through full analysis before this rulemaking proceeds further.

Best,
Sophia Simpson-Khan
Olympia, WA

text:
Re: Rescission of the Roadless Area Conservation Rule, Docket FS-2025-0001

The Southwest deserts, the West Coast, the Rockies, the East Coast, the Appalachians: I have hiked and camped across all of them, for perspective, clarity, my mental health, and to feel closer to my Creator. I am filing this comment to oppose the rescission of the 2001 Roadless Area Conservation Rule. Public lands should be managed to preserve the land, for people, not corporations. This proposal moves in exactly the opposite direction, and the agency's own numbers make that plain.

The economic case for rescission collapses under the agency's own data. The record before the agency states that "the total timber volume affected by this rule is less than 0.5 percent of total United States production, and the total oil and gas production from all National Forest System lands is currently about 0.4 percent of the current national production." Fractions that small cannot drive a decision of this magnitude. The agency's Cost Benefit Analysis projects timber revenue to the Forest Service of only $5.2 to $11.4 million a year, while projecting recreation losses of at least $6.1 million a year and a net present value ranging from -$92 million to +$199 million, a range that cannot establish a net benefit by any honest reading. Meanwhile, the Forest Service is already $6.9 billion behind on maintaining the roads it has, on a road budget of roughly $73 million a year. It makes no sense to build more roads when we cannot even fund what we already have. I certainly do not want my tax dollars used for logging and mining infrastructure. It is hard to square that spending with the same voices that decry subsidizing anything else. I ask that the agency reconcile this proposal with its own Cost Benefit Analysis and explain how an action whose numbers cannot establish a net benefit justifies expanding a road system already carrying a $6.9 billion maintenance backlog.

The rule the agency now proposes to eliminate already contains the flexibility it claims to need. The rule "generally banned road building subject to limited exceptions including: the preservation of 'reserved or outstanding rights' or discretionary Forest Service construction necessary for public health and safety. 36 C.F.R. Section 294.12(b)(1),(3)." If exceptions for public health, safety, and existing mineral rights are already written into the rule, the agency owes the public a specific accounting of which burdens remain unaddressed by those provisions, stated in quantified terms rather than asserted in the abstract.

Living in SoCal, I see wildfires repeatedly in places where there are not a lot of massive trees but rather invasive vegetation. These mountains are a massive hotbed for wildfires, and that is precisely why I am not convinced that logging decreases wildfire risk. My understanding is that most wildfires start near roads, and looking at burn scar maps, that really does seem to be the case. An agency serious about fire would not be building new roads into country that has none.

Water is a commodity we cannot afford to compromise. More than 7,000 municipal water intakes sit in watersheds fed by these roadless areas, and the agency's own analysis says roads and their facilities can produce up to 90 percent of the sediment from a timber sale. Fewer than 12 percent of those watersheds have impaired streams today. Opening them to roads puts that directly at risk.

This proposal was built to reach a predetermined conclusion. "Alternatives with more protection were dismissed as not responsive to the deregulatory executive orders, and the keep-boundaries option was cut because it 'would continue to restrict local decision-making discretion' and because analysing roadless values is 'an administrative and legal burden for the agency.'" A purpose-and-need statement written as deregulation forecloses exactly the comparison that NEPA requires. I ask that the agency restate the purpose and need in terms of actual forest conditions and analyse at least one protective alternative in full.

I want my kids to enjoy the public lands I have. I want my grandkids to enjoy them too. I do not want them to grow up in a mining and logging wasteland. Once it is gone, it is gone. We should be looking to restore and create more public lands, not surrender what remains of the last unroaded third of the national forests. The Forest Service held more than 600 public meetings and took 1.6 million comments to write the rule it now proposes to erase. It has held none to undo it. That asymmetry alone demands a full answer.

Sincerely,
Cora Cordova 
Pasadena, CA

text:
Re: Rescission of the Roadless Area Conservation Rule, Docket FS-2025-0001

Public lands should be managed to preserve nature and the natural processes that protect the environment. That is not a complicated position, but this proposal makes it harder to hold. I am filing this comment in opposition to the rescission of the 2001 Roadless Area Conservation Rule.

The agency justifies rescission in part on wildfire and fuels management grounds. Its own record undermines that justification. The agency's findings state that "Building a road into a forest at high risk from uncharacteristic wildfire effects could increase the incidence of human-caused fires. A human-caused wildland fire is nearly five times more likely to occur on essentially roaded lands than on essentially unroaded lands." If the goal is reducing ignition risk, opening roadless areas to road construction moves in the wrong direction. The agency should explain how the rescission can be squared with its own prior findings on fire occurrence, and it should reconcile this proposal with the ignition data in its own draft environmental impact statement, which reports far higher fire density on roaded land than inside the affected roadless areas.

The proposal is also justified on timber and energy economics. The agency's own record says that "the total timber volume affected by this rule is less than 0.5 percent of total United States production, and the total oil and gas production from all National Forest System lands is currently about 0.4 percent of the current national production." Those are not numbers that describe a national economic emergency. Meanwhile the agency's own Cost Benefit Analysis projects $5.2 to $11.4 million a year in timber revenue to the Forest Service against recreation losses of at least $6.1 million a year, with a net present value spanning -$92 million to +$199 million. That range does not establish a net benefit. And it does not account for the context the agency already knows: the road system it manages is $6.9 billion behind on maintenance, against a road budget of about $73 million a year. Building new roads into country that currently has none, when the agency cannot pay to maintain the roads it already has, is the wrong use of limited money. It is like building a new house because you never vacuumed. The agency must reconcile this proposal with an economic analysis that cannot demonstrate a net positive outcome, and it must explain on the record why expanding a road system already carrying a $6.9 billion maintenance backlog is a responsible use of public resources.

The proposal is also defended on permitting and administrative burden grounds. But the rule as written already provides exceptions. It "generally banned road building subject to limited exceptions including: the preservation of 'reserved or outstanding rights' or discretionary Forest Service construction necessary for public health and safety. 36 C.F.R. Section 294.12(b)(1),(3)." The agency has not explained which specific burdens are not already addressed by those existing exceptions, including those for existing mineral leases and community wildfire protection. The agency should identify those burdens specifically and quantify them.

Finally, the regulatory flexibility analysis certifies no significant impact on small entities. That conclusion is not credible. "The proposed rule certifies no significant impact on small entities while the DEIS names outfitters, guides and tour operators as affected and its own Cost Benefit Analysis books lost recreation benefit at a minimum of $6.1 million a year." The analysis reaches its no-impact conclusion by spreading that loss across every small firm in the sector nationally, rather than looking at the outfitters, guides and permit holders who actually operate in the affected areas. That is not an assessment; it is an averaging exercise designed to make a real impact disappear. The agency should withdraw the certification and conduct a genuine analysis of the small entities actually operating in the potentially affected roadless areas.

Nature and the natural processes that protect the environment deserve better than this. I ask that the agency address each of these points and enter its responses into the record.

Sincerely,
Sean P.
Provo, Utah

text:
Re: Rescission of the Roadless Area Conservation Rule, Docket FS-2025-0001

The forests in my state make me feel like a tourist in my own home, in the best sense. I am constantly drawn to photograph them, to capture something of what makes them what they are. That is why I am opposing the proposed rescission of the 2001 Roadless Area Conservation Rule, Docket FS-2025-0001. What the agency is proposing to discard is not bureaucratic surplus. It is the legal architecture that keeps these places worth photographing at all.

The wildfire rationale the agency offers for rescission is the one that troubles me most directly, because it runs against the agency's own record. The proposal suggests that opening roadless areas to road construction will help manage fire. The agency's prior findings say the opposite: "Building a road into a forest at high risk from uncharacteristic wildfire effects could increase the incidence of human-caused fires. A human-caused wildland fire is nearly five times more likely to occur on essentially roaded lands than on essentially unroaded lands." The forests I care about are the ones still intact enough to photograph in their essence, and the data the agency itself compiled shows that roading them raises ignition risk sharply. The agency must explain, directly and specifically, why this proposal departs from that prior finding, and how it reconciles the rescission with the ignition data in its own draft environmental impact statement.

The economic case for rescission is equally difficult to square with the agency's own numbers. The record already reflects that "the total timber volume affected by this rule is less than 0.5 percent of total United States production, and the total oil and gas production from all National Forest System lands is currently about 0.4 percent of the current national production." Against that backdrop, the agency projects $5.2 to $11.4 million a year in timber revenue to the Forest Service, set against recreation losses of at least $6.1 million a year, with a net present value ranging from -$92 million to +$199 million. The agency's own cost-benefit analysis cannot establish that the action produces a net benefit. The agency must reconcile that range of outcomes with a proposal to expand a road system that already carries a $6.9 billion maintenance backlog.

The proposal also argues that state-specific approaches can serve as a functional substitute for a single national rule. The agency has tried this before. The record reflects that "the USDA discussed its dissatisfaction with the Roadless Rule and highlighted its rejection of the Roadless Rule's 'inflexible one-size-fits-all nationwide rulemaking approach.' 70 Fed.Reg. at 25,656." What the record does not reflect is how a state-by-state framework avoids the conclusion the Ninth Circuit reached when the agency last attempted exactly this substitution, namely that local decision-making can incrementally erode nationally significant roadless values in ways a patchwork of state rules cannot prevent. The agency needs to address that history and explain what is structurally different this time.

Finally, the administrative burden argument does not survive contact with the rule's actual text. The rule as written already provides that it "generally banned road building subject to limited exceptions including: the preservation of 'reserved or outstanding rights' or discretionary Forest Service construction necessary for public health and safety. 36 C.F.R. Section 294.12(b)(1),(3)." Exceptions for public health and safety, existing mineral leases, and community wildfire protection are already embedded in the rule the agency now calls unworkable. The agency has not identified which specific operational needs fall outside those exceptions, and it has not quantified the burden of any gap that genuinely exists. It should do both, on the record, before proceeding any further with this rescission.

Sincerely,
Josiah Morgan
Snohomish, Washington

text:
Subject: Oppose rescission of the 2001 Roadless Rule – Docket FS-2025-0001
I am a Forest Service retiree with a career in wildlife and recreation management in Region 6 and Region 8. Now, as a volunteer conservationist and enthusiastic backcountry recreationist that depends on a healthy and robust outdoor recreation economy, I oppose the proposed rescission of the 2001 Roadless Area Conservation Rule.
The Roadless Rule has been an effective, durable baseline that protects water quality, wildlife habitat, carbon storage, and high-value backcountry recreation across tens of millions of acres. If the Roadless Rule is repealed and decisions are made only at the local level, protection will become fragmented and uneven. That weakens the overall conservation framework, without any credible evidence that the national rule itself is what limits our ability to address forest health or wildfire risks.
There are 370,000 miles of roads in the National Forest System with a maintenance backlog of $10.8 billion. 55% of this inventory is older poorly located and/or maintained roads that cause erosion and stream sedimentation. The result is reduced water quality, barriers to fish migration, and/or public safety hazards. We need to take care of the roads we already have including closing and rehabilitating damaging road systems, not add more roads that we don’t have the funding or personnel to maintain.
The NOI cites changing conditions, wildfire, insects, disease, and WUI growth. Those realities deserve targeted, site-specific tools. They do not require removing the national safeguards that prevent road building and timber extraction in places where intact landscapes are the very asset we are trying to conserve. Existing authorities within the Roadless Rule under 36 CFR 294 12(b) and 13(b) with environmental review, allow for the necessary exceptions for protection of public health and safety from natural disasters such as wildfire and floods as well as for wildlife/T&E species habitat restoration/maintenance. 
Before rescinding the rule, the EIS should rigorously analyze: (1) alternatives that retain the Roadless baseline while enabling time-bounded, decommission-on-completion access for hazard reduction near communities; (2) lifecycle costs and maintenance liabilities of any new roads; (3) impacts to municipal watersheds, fisheries, and backcountry economies; and (4) cumulative effects from increased access on invasive spread and fragmentation.
Finally, the scoping window is not sufficient for meaningful participation in an action of this magnitude. The comment period should have been 90 days and there should have been regional public meetings. The draft EIS should include a robust No Action and much better crafted Modified Roadless alternative.
Thank you for considering these comments.
Alan R. McPherson

text:
Re: Rescission of the Roadless Area Conservation Rule, Docket FS-2025-0001

The leasing and exploitation of these lands will despoil the birthright of future generations. No one has the right to do that. I am submitting this comment in opposition to the proposed rescission of the 2001 Roadless Area Conservation Rule, Docket FS-2025-0001. Our public lands should be managed for preservation, to protect wild spaces and the ecosystems they support. What follows explains why this proposal fails that standard and why it should be withdrawn.

The most serious problem with this rulemaking is structural. The agency wrote its purpose as a deregulatory exercise and then dismissed every alternative that did not serve that predetermined end. The DEIS states that Alternatives with more protection were dismissed as not responsive to the deregulatory executive orders, and the keep-boundaries option was cut because it "would continue to restrict local decision-making discretion" and because analysing roadless values is "an administrative and legal burden for the agency." A purpose stated as deregulation forecloses the comparative analysis that NEPA exists to require. No legitimate range of alternatives was ever considered, because alternatives that protected roadless character were ruled out before analysis began rather than evaluated and found wanting. I ask that the agency restate the purpose and need in terms of actual forest conditions and analyse at least one fully protective alternative before proceeding further.

The wildfire rationale that appears throughout public discussion of this proposal does not survive contact with the agency's own numbers. The purpose and need is to reduce regulatory burden and return decisionmaking to local officials. Overlap with the wildland-urban interface as defined by HFRA is 9.8 million acres, 24 percent of the affected area, and the DEIS says the benefits of added fuel-management access "would likely be modest and localized." The agency itself constructed a WUI-targeted alternative that would have addressed the fire argument without eliminating protections across the remaining 76 percent of affected acreage, and then rejected it. Nationwide rescission cannot be justified by a rationale the agency's own document describes as modest and localized. The agency must explain in this docket why it chose full rescission over the targeted alternative it built and discarded.

The exceptions argument the agency offers is circular in a way the DEIS itself inadvertently admits. The 2001 rule's exceptions were expected to be infrequent by design; their infrequent use is now offered as evidence of failure, in a document that concedes "the rule's intent for infrequent use." A rule working exactly as designed is not a defect. Before this proceeding goes further, the agency should publish the actual counts of exception requests, approvals, denials, and processing times, so the public can evaluate whether the mechanism failed or whether the agency simply dislikes the answer it was designed to produce.

The watersheds these lands support must be left pristine and unpolluted. The DEIS acknowledges that Approximately 24 million people use water originating within the potentially affected roadless areas, through more than 7,000 municipal intakes, and less than 12 percent of these watersheds are currently impaired. That low impairment rate is not an argument for change. It is the argument against it. The agency responds to this concern by asserting that forest plans will address drinking water sources, but it identifies no enforceable provision in any forest plan that is equivalent to what the current rule provides. The agency must identify, forest by forest, which specific plan provisions it considers equivalent to 36 CFR 294.12 and 294.13 for municipal watersheds, so that the public and reviewing courts can evaluate whether the asserted protection is real.

The Forest Service held more than 600 public meetings and received 1.6 million comments before issuing the 2001 rule. It has held none to undo it. These are the last unroaded third of the national forests. A logged stand grows back. A road does not. The agency has not demonstrated that rescission is necessary, that alternatives were fairly considered, or that the protections it proposes to remove will be replaced by anything enforceable. The proposed rescission should not proceed.

Sincerely,
John Pittman
New York, NY

text:
Re: Rescission of the Roadless Area Conservation Rule, Docket FS-2025-0001

The ability to hike and camp further into uncivilized areas, to experience something beyond the reach of roads, is precisely what is at stake here. That is what I value in our public lands, and that is what this proposal would take away from U.S. citizens at costs that are wrong for us.

The economic case for rescission does not survive the agency's own numbers. The record states that "the total timber volume affected by this rule is less than 0.5 percent of total United States production, and the total oil and gas production from all National Forest System lands is currently about 0.4 percent of the current national production." Against that marginal commercial stake, the agency's own Cost Benefit Analysis projects timber revenue to the Forest Service of only $5.2 to $11.4 million a year, set against recreation losses of at least $6.1 million a year and a net present value ranging from -$92 million to +$199 million. That range does not establish a net benefit. It establishes uncertainty. And expanding a road system already carrying a $6.9 billion maintenance backlog into that uncertainty is a choice the agency has not adequately justified. I ask the agency to reconcile this proposal with those figures and explain how an action whose own analysis cannot confirm a positive return warrants proceeding at all.

The proposal also argues for replacing the national rule with state-specific approaches, but the agency has been down that road before. The record quotes the agency's own prior position, in which "the USDA discussed its dissatisfaction with the Roadless Rule and highlighted its rejection of the Roadless Rule's 'inflexible one-size-fits-all' nationwide rulemaking approach.' 70 Fed.Reg. at 25,656." That prior attempt at a state-by-state substitution was reviewed by the Ninth Circuit, which found deficiencies the agency has not addressed in this proposal. The agency must explain how this new proposal avoids repeating those same failures, and why local decision-making, which the agency's own record acknowledges can incrementally erode nationally significant roadless values, is now adequate where it was not before.

On the question of statutory authority, the agency's position is weakened further by what courts have already decided. The Tenth Circuit, after full review, held: "Exercising jurisdiction pursuant to 28 U.S.C. Section 1291, we REVERSE the district court's order granting Plaintiffs declaratory relief and issuing a permanent injunction, and REMAND the case for the district court to vacate the permanent injunction." That court found the 2001 rule to be within the authority Congress granted under the Organic Act and the Multiple-Use Sustained-Yield Act, and found that it did not create de facto wilderness. If the agency now holds a contrary view of its own statutory authority, it must state that position plainly and explain its legal basis in the record.

Finally, many of the administrative burdens cited to justify rescission are not clearly distinct from what the existing rule already accommodates. The rule as written "generally banned road building subject to limited exceptions including: the preservation of 'reserved or outstanding rights' or discretionary Forest Service construction necessary for public health and safety. 36 C.F.R. Section 294.12(b)(1),(3)." The rule also carries existing exceptions touching mineral leases and community wildfire protection. The agency has not identified which specific burdens fall outside those existing provisions, nor has it quantified them. Before rescinding a rule that protects what I and millions of other citizens go to public lands for, the agency should be required to name those burdens with precision and put numbers behind them.

I am asking that the agency respond to each of these points in the record before any final action is taken.

Sincerely,
Heather Kinney
Missouri

text:
Re: Rescission of the Roadless Area Conservation Rule, Docket FS-2025-0001

The air is clean and the animals and trees are still there. Those are not small things. I hike throughout our country. I watch bears, foxes, beavers, wolves, deer, coyotes, rabbits, squirrels, opossums, and birds of all kinds, wherever I go. I photograph everything. I am writing this comment because I want the agency to understand what is at stake in the real world before it rescinds the 2001 Roadless Area Conservation Rule.

The agency's own record on fire destroys its own justification. The proposal gestures toward wildfire management as a reason to open these areas to road building. But the agency already found, in its own analysis, that "Building a road into a forest at high risk from uncharacteristic wildfire effects could increase the incidence of human-caused fires. A human-caused wildland fire is nearly five times more likely to occur on essentially roaded lands than on essentially unroaded lands." I have lived through fire seasons. I have seen people and animals with nowhere to go. I have seen what it does to air quality for every living thing. I have seen trees destroyed, the same trees that cool the earth and provide shade for all. The agency must explain on the record why this proposal departs from its own prior finding that roads increase fire occurrence, and it must reconcile the rescission with the ignition data in DEIS Table 21, which reports far higher fire density on roaded land than inside the affected roadless areas.

California alone holds 381 inventoried roadless areas totaling 4,389,760 acres, and 1,034 municipal water intakes sit in watersheds containing affected roadless areas across the Pacific Southwest region. These are areas where water starts clean. You destroy the source where you get water and there is no guarantee you can clean it enough after the fact to drink or use. The agency's own record notes that roads and their facilities can produce up to 90 percent of the sediment from a timber sale. Opening these areas to roads is a choice to put that water at risk for communities who depend on it. I ask the agency to explain, on the record, how it weighs this risk against the benefits it claims, and to address what happens to those water supplies once the protection is gone.

The deer and the bears I look for require something the proposal would take away: unroaded security. The agency's own analysis acknowledges that roads built for extraction may have altered mule deer migration routes and increased their movement speed. For bears, the agency cites its own grizzly recovery record finding that contact and conflict increase with even secondary unpaved roads, and that shooting, habituation, and food reward all rise with road use in that habitat. The record also states that wide-ranging mammals "have suffered habitat loss and the extirpation or fragmentation of their populations." These are not abstract concerns. They describe what happens to the animals I spend my life looking for. The agency must address, concretely, what mitigation it proposes for wildlife that the existing rule's protections have kept intact.

On the economics: "the total timber volume affected by this rule is less than 0.5 percent of total United States production, and the total oil and gas production from all National Forest System lands is currently about 0.4 percent of the current national production." These are the agency's own words. Using my money to build new roads into country that has none, when the agency is already $6.9 billion behind on maintaining the roads it already has on a road budget of about $73 million a year, would be incompetent and irresponsible. The agency must reconcile the proposal with an economic record whose own cost-benefit analysis cannot establish a net benefit, and explain how expanding an already failing road system serves the public interest.

Finally, a court already answered the authority question. The Tenth Circuit's holding, reversing the district court and remanding for vacatur of the injunction, is in the record: "Exercising jurisdiction pursuant to 28 U.S.C. Section 1291, we REVERSE the district court's order granting Plaintiffs declaratory relief and issuing a permanent injunction, and REMAND the case for the district court to vacate the permanent injunction." The proposal argues the 2001 rule exceeded statutory authority. The courts that reviewed that question disagreed. The agency must address the Tenth Circuit's holding and explain the basis for any contrary position.

Our public lands should be managed for the care, protection, and growth of native plants and wildlife. That is what these areas do now. I oppose rescission of the 2001 Roadless Area Conservation Rule.

Sincerely,
Lisa Green
Thousand Oaks, CA

text:
To the USDA Roadless Rule Team:

As a Coloradan, and a wildlife enthusiast, I believe the 2001 rule is the single most important land management instrument and the threat of its removal is not only catastrophic but infuriating.

Every year, I take a fall trip to explore these beautiful mountains and every year I am left with wonder. Seeing new wildlife, a new sunset, a new plant, a riverbed - it never ceases to amaze me. The protection of these ecosystems are imperative for us, but also for all.

Being able to backpack through these undisturbed mountains and connect with other life is one of the few things that bring me joy and peace in such a hectic world. Roads end that possibility.

Regarding the Mount Antero in the Pike & San Isabel NFs-

Alpine and Subalpine Climate Refugia Connectivity — The area spans from 13,600 feet to 14,276 feet across multiple subalpine and alpine ecosystem types—Rocky Mountain subalpine spruce-fir forest, alpine tundra, and bristlecone pine woodland—creating an intact elevational gradient that allows species to shift their ranges as climate conditions change. This vertical connectivity is critical as warming temperatures push suitable habitat upslope; species dependent on cool conditions can only persist if they can move continuously to higher elevations without fragmentation. Road construction fragments this gradient by creating edge effects, altering microclimate through canopy removal, and introducing invasive species along disturbed corridors, which would trap populations in lower-elevation refugia that are becoming increasingly unsuitable.

DEIS Narrative Exceeds the 150-Page Statutory Limit With No Extraordinary-Complexity Determination on the Record

The Draft EIS exceeds the statutory page limit and contains no determination authorizing it to do so.

Volume I of the Draft EIS is 333 pages. Its narrative text runs from the Introduction at page 9 through page 248. References Cited occupies pages 249 through 285, and the List of Appendices and Appendices 1 through 5 occupy pages 286 through 333. Excluding citations and appendices, as the statute directs, the environmental impact statement is therefore approximately 240 pages long.

The applicable limit is 150 pages. 42 U.S.C. 4336a, enacted by the Fiscal Responsibility Act of 2023, limits an environmental impact statement to 150 pages excluding citations and appendices, and permits 300 pages only where the proposed agency action is of extraordinary complexity. USDA's NEPA procedures implement the same limits at 7 CFR 1b.7(a) and (i). The Draft EIS expressly adopts those procedures, stating at page 9 that the Forest Service "has prepared this draft environmental impact statement (EIS) in compliance with the National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA) and other relevant laws and regulations," and that "all references to 7 CFR 1b within this document refer to the interim rule."

The document therefore exceeds the 150-page limit by approximately 90 pages. The only lawful basis for an environmental impact statement of this length is a determination that the proposed action is of extraordinary complexity. Volume I contains no such determination. The phrases "extraordinary complexity," "page limit," and "Fiscal Responsibility Act" do not appear anywhere in the document, and 42 U.S.C. 4336a is cited nowhere in it. The Draft EIS asserts compliance with "other relevant laws and regulations" while exceeding the one quantitative constraint those laws place on the document itself, and without invoking the exception that would authorize the excess.

This is not a matter of formatting. The page limit operates together with 7 CFR 1b.7(i), which directs that issues not of a substantive nature receive the briefest possible discussion. A ceiling of 150 pages applied to a rescission affecting approximately 44.7 million acres of National Forest System lands compels the agency to compress its effects analysis, and the extent of that compression depends directly on which ceiling the responsible official was working to. A document written to 150 pages must omit substantially more analysis than one written to 300. The public reading this Draft EIS cannot tell which constraint shaped it, because the document never says - and the difference is roughly 90 pages of effects analysis across 44.7 million acres.

I request that the responsible official make and document the extraordinary-complexity determination required by 42 U.S.C. 4336a and 7 CFR 1b.7(a) as the predicate for a Final EIS exceeding 150 pages, or, if no such determination is made, that the Final EIS text comply with the 150-page limit. Under 7 CFR 1b.7(f)(3), the response to this comment should cite where in the Final EIS or the supporting proposal record that determination is accounted for.

A rule that has survived twenty-five years, multiple administrations, and repeated judicial review deserves more deference than this.

CommentID: RLC-20261006-9WBQV3

text:
I am writing to oppose the proposed rescission of the 2001 Roadless Area Conservation Rule (36 CFR 294, Subpart B, docket FS-2025-0001, RIN 0596-AD66), and to ask the Department to withdraw this proposal and keep the rule in effect, including for the Tongass National Forest.

I was born and raised in Sitka and have lived in Southeast Alaska my entire life. I expect to remain here for the rest of it. The Tongass National Forest is not scenery to me; it is where my family gets much of its food. All of the meat and salmon we eat comes from hunting and fishing in the Tongass, and the roadless areas this proposal would leave unprotected are exactly where it comes from. Roadless watersheds spawn the salmon that support Southeast Alaska's commercial fleets and produce the deer that fill freezers across the region. This proposal puts the long-term health of those watersheds on the table for, at best, a marginal and short-lived expansion of logging.

I would like to address the Department's stated reasons for the rescission directly.

The notice argues that rescission restores local flexibility and that land management plans will protect roadless values. But the notice itself shows how narrow that argument is. It states that locatable mineral exploration and development is generally accompanied by an access right and that no changes are anticipated there, and hydropower, transmission, and other uses already proceed in roadless areas. What the rescission actually changes is one-directional: by the Department's own estimate, it opens about 18.2 million acres (45.5 percent of affected roadless lands) to permanent road construction where plans now prohibit it, and about 4.8 million forested roadless acres to timber harvest. A flexibility that only ever moves toward more roads and logging is not balance; it is a one-way ratchet.

The Department's own economic analysis makes the same case. The best it can project is $4.6 to $10.6 million per year for the timber industry and a 5 to 10 percent increase in national forest sawtimber harvest the notice itself describes as unlikely, set against total annual impacts that could exceed $100 million and recreation losses of $6.1 million per year. Meanwhile, the Forest Service carries a $6.9 billion deferred maintenance backlog on the roads and bridges it already has. An agency that cannot maintain its existing roads should not be carving new ones into roadless watersheds it will then be unable to care for.

In Southeast Alaska the arithmetic is even more lopsided. Large-scale logging has already taken much of the Tongass's most valuable old growth, and the remaining roadless areas are where the fish and wildlife that anchor our region still hold on. Our economy runs on wild fish and wild places: commercial fishing, tourism, and subsistence harvest, all of which depend on intact watersheds. The notice acknowledges that near-term logging gains would be "modest and localized" and that significant effects on commercial fishing are not expected in the short term, but damage to salmon habitat and wildlife from new road networks is cumulative and effectively permanent, falling on the people who live here long after any cost-benefit window has closed.

I also want to address the wildfire argument, because it is the one most likely to be offered for a national rescission. Whatever the case for active management in the fire-prone interior West, the Tongass is a temperate rainforest; its pressures are roads and logging, not catastrophic wildfire. A national rescission pitched to Western fire conditions should not be the instrument that opens Southeast Alaska's roadless rainforest. And where fuels work near communities is genuinely needed, the notice's own figures identify 9.8 million acres of wildland-urban interface overlapping roadless areas, so that work can proceed without stripping protections everywhere at once.

Finally, a word on process. The 2025 notice of intent drew more than 220,000 comments on behalf of over 625,000 individuals and organizations, and the majority of Tribes consulted oppose the rescission as a threat to their rights and the ecological health of their homelands. The 2001 Rule followed one of the most extensive public involvement processes in the Forest Service's history. These roadless lands belong to all Americans, including those who will never visit them and generations not yet born. Removing their protection over this record of public and Tribal objection is not local decisionmaking; it is a single national decision handed down against it.

For these reasons, I urge the Department to withdraw this proposed rescission. If it proceeds notwithstanding, I ask that it complete a rigorous ANILCA Section 810 subsistence analysis before any decision, hold hearings genuinely accessible to Southeast Alaska communities, and give the results real weight in the final rule.

Thank you for considering my comments.

Blake Laperriere
Sitka, Alaska

text:
I oppose the proposed rescission of the 2001 Roadless Area Conservation Rule and request that the Forest Service retain it. If specific provisions prevent necessary wildfire-risk-reduction or restoration work, those constraints should be addressed through targeted amendments rather than eliminating protections nationwide.

The wildfire rationale does not appear to justify nationwide rescission. The existing Rule already provides exceptions for road construction when necessary to protect public health and safety from imminent threats such as wildfire and allows qualifying vegetation management for ecosystem restoration and reduction of uncharacteristic wildfire effects.

Forest Service research also raises questions about whether roadlessness is actually a significant barrier to fuels management. Healey (2020), *Long-term forest health implications of roadlessness*, found that fuel-management activities occurred more frequently per unit area in roadless lands, although individual treatments in roaded areas tended to be larger. More recent research identifies an important unintended consequence. Aplet, Hartger, and Dietz (2026), analyzing wildfire occurrence from 1992–2024 across the contiguous United States, found approximately **1.97 wildfire ignitions per 1,000 hectares in inventoried roadless areas compared with 7.99 per 1,000 hectares within 50 meters of roads**. Roads can facilitate suppression access, but expanding roads into currently roadless areas may also increase human-caused wildfire ignitions.

Before rescinding the Rule, the Forest Service should quantify how many wildfire-risk-reduction or restoration projects have actually been prevented by the Roadless Rule and could not proceed under existing exceptions. It should also evaluate whether increased ignition risk from additional road access could offset anticipated wildfire-management benefits.

Rescission could also impose significant long-term watershed and fiscal costs. Roads alter runoff pathways, concentrate drainage, increase erosion and sediment delivery, and create potential failure points at stream crossings. Because inventoried roadless areas occur within hundreds of major watersheds, their value includes drinking-water-source protection, reduced sedimentation, aquatic-habitat protection, and maintenance of watershed function.

New roads also create continuing taxpayer obligations for drainage and culvert maintenance, erosion control, reconstruction, and eventual decommissioning. These lifecycle costs should be evaluated alongside any projected economic benefits of increased access.

If the agency's concern is that the Rule limits management in particular high-risk landscapes, nationwide rescission is unnecessarily broad. A more reasonable alternative is to retain the national conservation baseline while allowing narrowly tailored, science-based exceptions where the Forest Service demonstrates that road construction is necessary for public safety, community wildfire protection, or ecological restoration; less damaging alternatives are inadequate; and wildfire-ignition, watershed, and lifecycle infrastructure costs have been evaluated.

Wildfire risk warrants active and thoughtful forest management, but it does not demonstrate a need to eliminate roadless protections nationwide. Available evidence indicates that roadless status has not prevented substantial fuels management and that additional road access may itself increase wildfire ignitions. Combined with the long-term watershed and infrastructure costs of expanding the road network, these considerations favor targeted management solutions rather than nationwide rescission.

Thank you for considering these comments.

text:
Re: Rescission of the Roadless Area Conservation Rule, Docket FS-2025-0001

Nature does not wait for process, and the quiet it takes to photograph private moments in a place like Reister Canyon, a roadless area of 5,897 acres in the Mendocino NF in California, is not renewable the way a logged stand is. Roads persist. That is the argument the agency itself made when it spent years holding more than 600 public meetings and receiving 1.6 million comments to write the rule it now proposes to rescind without holding a single equivalent proceeding. These roadless forests need to be protected for future generations, and this proposal does not make that case.

The wildfire rationale the agency offers deserves direct scrutiny. The agency's own record states: "Building a road into a forest at high risk from uncharacteristic wildfire effects could increase the incidence of human-caused fires. A human-caused wildland fire is nearly five times more likely to occur on essentially roaded lands than on essentially unroaded lands." I ask that the agency to explain why the proposal departs from those prior findings on fire occurrence and fuel treatment, and that it reconcile the rescission with the ignition data in its own DEIS Table 21, which reports far higher fire density on roaded land than inside the affected roadless areas.

The economic case is no stronger. The agency's own record states: "the total timber volume affected by this rule is less than 0.5 percent of total United States production, and the total oil and gas production from all National Forest System lands is currently about 0.4 percent of the current national production." Against projected timber revenue of $5.2 to $11.4 million a year to the Forest Service, the agency's own Cost Benefit Analysis books recreation losses of at least $6.1 million a year and a net present value ranging from -$92 million to +$199 million. A range that spans negative territory is not a demonstrated benefit. The agency must explain how an action whose own analysis cannot establish a net gain justifies expanding a road system already carrying a $6.9 billion maintenance backlog.

The regulatory flexibility certification is similarly unsupported. The proposed rule certifies no significant impact on small entities while the DEIS names outfitters, guides and tour operators as affected and its own Cost Benefit Analysis books lost recreation benefit at a minimum of $6.1 million a year. That conclusion is reached by spreading losses across every small firm in the sector nationally rather than looking at the guides and outfitters actually holding permits in the affected areas. The certification should be withdrawn and the analysis redone for the entities actually operating in the places at issue.

Finally, the agency cannot in good conscience declare plan amendments beyond the scope of this proposal and then solicit comment on them. The proposed rule concedes that subsequent land management plan amendments and revisions “could increase the area where timber harvest and road construction would be allowed,” declares changes to plans beyond the scope of the proposal, and then requests public comment on them (91 FR 53830). That is not a defensible analytical boundary. The foreseeable plan-amendment scenario, including expanded timber harvest area, belongs inside this action's environmental review, not outside it.

Sincerely,
Jackie Biegel
Los Angeles, CA

text:
Re: Rescission of the Roadless Area Conservation Rule, Docket FS-2025-0001

The forests I seek out for hiking, camping, and photography are public lands where nature rules and cars are not allowed to go. What I look for through a lens is a scene without power lines, concrete, or construction. The 2001 Roadless Area Conservation Rule protects exactly that kind of country, and I am filing this comment to oppose its rescission under Docket FS-2025-0001.

The agency's own economic data does not support this action. The record states that "the total timber volume affected by this rule is less than 0.5 percent of total United States production, and the total oil and gas production from all National Forest System lands is currently about 0.4 percent of the current national production." Against that marginal contribution, the agency's own Cost Benefit Analysis projects timber revenue to the Forest Service of only $5.2 to $11.4 million a year, recreation losses of at least $6.1 million a year, and a net present value range spanning negative $92 million to positive $199 million. That spread cannot establish a net benefit. My question, which I ask the agency to answer squarely in this record, is how an action whose own analysis cannot demonstrate a positive return justifies adding new roads to a system already carrying a $6.9 billion maintenance backlog.

My thinking on the maintenance backlog follows from simple priorities I hold as a citizen. We have gutted healthcare and education while facilitating a war overseas. If we do not have money to fund our citizens' health and education, why are we actively looking for new ways to spend? What happened to America first? We need to care for what we already have before expanding into something new. The Forest Service road budget is approximately $73 million a year against that $6.9 billion deficit. I ask that the agency reconcile its road-expansion rationale with those numbers before this docket closes.

The regulatory flexibility certification compounds the problem. "The proposed rule certifies no significant impact on small entities while the DEIS names outfitters, guides and tour operators as affected and its own Cost Benefit Analysis books lost recreation benefit at a minimum of $6.1 million a year." The supporting analysis reaches its no-impact conclusion by spreading the loss across every small firm in the sector nationally, rather than examining the outfitters and guides who actually hold permits in the affected areas. The agency concedes some of those firms may lose these receipts. The certification should be withdrawn and the impact assessed on the businesses actually operating in the potentially affected roadless areas, not the national average firm. I ask that the agency explain why the current certification satisfies its obligations under the Regulatory Flexibility Act.

The reliance-interest analysis is absent. "The proposal solicits 'any reliance interests in the current rule that could be affected by this proposal' (91 FR 53830-31), and the Cost Benefit Analysis weighs none." This comment is exactly such an interest. The places I rely on for the kind of photography and hiking that depends on the absence of roads, power lines, and construction are protected under the current rule. When an agency changes course it must assess what its prior policy created. I ask that the agency identify and weigh the reliance interests described in the comments it receives, including this one, before it finalizes any rescission.

Finally, the agency's own fire data points in the wrong direction. "Human-caused ignition density is 22.4 fires per million acres per year on roaded National Forest System land against 3.0 inside the affected roadless areas (DEIS Table 21, 2014–2024), and the DEIS states that human-caused ignitions increase in abundance with proximity to roads." The effects analysis concedes that road access could increase the number and frequency of wildfires. The agency has not quantified the expected increase in human-caused ignitions that new road access would bring, nor has it weighed that increase against its claimed reduction in wildfire hazard. Those numbers belong in this record before a final decision is made.

Sincerely,
Rachel Dark
Austin, Texas

text: NEPA requires agencies to take a hard look at both the beneficial and adverse consequences of a proposed action. The DEIS fails to provide a balanced and legally adequate analysis of the economic and environmental consequences of rescinding the Roadless Rule. Throughout the document, the Forest Service emphasizes potential benefits associated with expanded management flexibility, timber harvest, road construction, and resource extraction. However, the DEIS does not provide a corresponding quantitative assessment of the economic value currently provided by intact Inventoried Roadless Areas, nor does it evaluate whether those values would be diminished by repeal of the Rule.

text:
Re: Rescission of the Roadless Area Conservation Rule, Docket FS-2025-0001

The peace and serenity of Grand Mesa National Forest is not incidental to my life; it is part of it. I hike there, and I farm downstream from it. All of my drinking water and agricultural irrigation water comes from that national forest watershed. Clean, healthy, intact, and undeveloped national forest is critical to my health and livelihood. The agency's proposal to rescind the 2001 Roadless Area Conservation Rule puts both at risk, and the agency's own record does not support what it is doing.

The wildfire justification for rescission is the place to start, because the agency's own findings undercut it most directly. The record states: "Building a road into a forest at high risk from uncharacteristic wildfire effects could increase the incidence of human-caused fires. A human-caused wildland fire is nearly five times more likely to occur on essentially roaded lands than on essentially unroaded lands." Living through wildfire year after year is, as I can only describe it, scary to say the least. Our quality of life is affected by the smoke, making it difficult to breathe and go outside. When the agency uses wildfire management as a rationale for opening roadless areas to road construction, it owes the public a direct reconciliation of that rationale with its own prior findings on ignition risk. I ask that the agency explain why the proposal departs from those findings and reconcile the rescission with the ignition data in its own draft environmental impact statement.

That same draft environmental impact statement is more specific still: "Human-caused ignition density is 22.4 fires per million acres per year on roaded National Forest System land against 3.0 inside the affected roadless areas (DEIS Table 21, 2014–2024), and the DEIS states that human-caused ignitions increase in abundance with proximity to roads." The claimed wildfire benefit of rescission cannot be taken at face value alongside numbers like those. The agency must quantify the expected increase in human-caused ignitions that new road access would produce and weigh that increase against the claimed reduction in wildfire hazard, openly, in the record.

Water is where this becomes a matter of survival for me, not sentiment. The agency's own analysis acknowledges that roads and their facilities can produce up to 90 percent of the sediment from a timber sale. My water supply, for drinking and for irrigating the farm that sustains my livelihood, begins in the national forest upstream from me. Increased sedimentation from road construction is not an abstraction. I ask that the agency address specifically how the rescission protects, rather than degrades, the water quality flowing from roadless watersheds to downstream agricultural and municipal users who depend on them.

The economic analysis accompanying this proposal also fails on its own terms. "The proposed rule certifies no significant impact on small entities while the DEIS names outfitters, guides and tour operators as affected and its own Cost Benefit Analysis books lost recreation benefit at a minimum of $6.1 million a year." That certification is reached by spreading the projected loss across every small firm in the sector nationally, rather than examining the outfitters, guides, and tour operators who actually hold permits in the affected areas. That method conceals harm by averaging it away. The agency should withdraw the certification and assess the impact on the businesses actually operating inside the areas this rescission would affect.

Finally, the agency has explicitly invited public comment on reliance interests. "The proposal solicits 'any reliance interests in the current rule that could be affected by this proposal' (91 FR 53830-31), and the Cost Benefit Analysis weighs none." My farm, my water supply, and my decision to remain and work where I do have all been shaped in part by the protections the 2001 rule provides. Soliciting reliance interests while the cost-benefit analysis assigns them no weight is not analysis. The agency must identify and genuinely weigh the reliance interests described in the comments it receives, including this one, before any final action is taken.

Sincerely,
Melissa Newell
Cedaredge, CO

text:
Re: Rescission of the Roadless Area Conservation Rule, Docket FS-2025-0001

My livelihood runs throughout the Quinault region. I lead foraging tours there as part of my business, and the South Quinault roadless area, all 11,081 acres of it in the Olympic National Forest, is the ground that business stands on. This area is home to the largest trees in the last protected temperate rainforest in the lower 48 states. (I have the LiDAR data to prove it). Logging here is a temporary boost to the local economy for some and a devastating loss for others. Keeping the roadless rule intact for this place guarantees economic wellbeing for generations to come. I am asking this agency to withdraw the proposed rescission of the 2001 Roadless Area Conservation Rule, and I am asking it to answer me this time. No one responded when I wrote about this in 2025, and that silence is not an answer.

The fire argument cuts against the proposal, not for it. The agency's own record states: "Building a road into a forest at high risk from uncharacteristic wildfire effects could increase the incidence of human-caused fires. A human-caused wildland fire is nearly five times more likely to occur on essentially roaded lands than on essentially unroaded lands." Roading the Quinault region would increase the possibility of fire. That is not my speculation. That is what the agency's own draft environmental impact statement shows. I ask that the agency explain why the proposal departs from those findings, and that it reconcile the rescission with the ignition data in DEIS Table 21, which reports far higher fire density on roaded land than inside the affected roadless areas.

The proposal cannot establish that the economics add up. The agency's own record states that "the total timber volume affected by this rule is less than 0.5 percent of total United States production, and the total oil and gas production from all National Forest System lands is currently about 0.4 percent of the current national production." Against that marginal production figure, the agency's own Cost Benefit Analysis projects timber revenue to the Forest Service of $5.2 to $11.4 million a year, recreation losses of at least $6.1 million a year, and a net present value spanning negative $92 million to positive $199 million. A road system already carrying a $6.9 billion maintenance backlog would be expanded for a return the agency cannot demonstrate is positive. Roading the South Quinault area would destroy my business as a tour guide in a currently unroaded area and would negatively affect the hiking trails my customers rely on. The agency must reconcile those numbers on the record and explain how an action whose own analysis cannot establish a net benefit justifies this rescission.

The proposal also must reckon with what the existing rule already allows. The 2001 rule did not ban all road construction. It included exceptions for public health and safety, for reserved or outstanding rights, and for existing uses. The proposal justifies rescission on permitting and administrative burden grounds, but it does not identify which specific burdens are not already addressed by those exceptions. Our community gets its drinking water from the Quinault region. Across the Pacific Northwest, 1,522 municipal water intakes sit in watersheds containing affected roadless areas. The public health and safety exception was written for exactly those stakes. The agency should identify on the record which burdens it claims are unmet by existing exceptions, and it should quantify them.

Finally, the agency's own record documents that elk survival rates increased during a road closure and decreased when the gates were removed, and that elk avoid roads and select unroaded habitat. The proposal offers no population-level projection for big game. The South Quinault area is part of a functioning ecosystem. A rule change with documented effects on wildlife behavior demands that the agency project what those effects mean at the population level before any final action is taken.

I make my livelihood in this region. The mushrooms I forage and the tours I lead depend on this place staying whole. What the agency treats as an administrative question is, for me and for my community, a practical one: whether the water is clean, whether the forest stands, whether the business survives. I expect a substantive response in this docket.

Sincerely,
Matt Houghton
Quinault, WA

text:
Re: Rescission of the Roadless Area Conservation Rule, Docket FS-2025-0001

The birds, deer, and occasional bear I watch in the Cherokee National Forest are the reason I am filing this comment. The proposal before the agency would end the protection that keeps those animals and that forest intact, and the agency's own analysis explains why that outcome is predictable and serious.

The Cherokee holds 18 inventoried roadless areas totaling 84,881 acres. The Joyce Kilmer Slickrock Addition, 1,396 of those acres, is one of the most beautiful and diverse forests in the eastern United States. Degrading it would be a real tragedy for present and future generations. The southern Appalachians are an evolutionary crossroads where more tree species grow than in all of northern Europe, and the roadless pockets within the Cherokee, small as they are individually, carry disproportionate biodiversity precisely because they have been left alone. Public lands are for the benefit of all people and should not be opened to commercial interests that will destroy the natural condition of the forests. That is the principle the 2001 rule embodies, and I oppose its rescission.

The birds I watch in the Cherokee are directly implicated by what the agency's own literature review found and then declined to act on. The DEIS cites the findings that bird richness declines with road presence in forested habitat, and that road-noise experiments in a roadless area cut bird abundance by over a quarter, with 31 percent of species avoiding the noise entirely. The DEIS also cites the finding that habitat fragmentation reduces biodiversity by 13 to 75 percent. That range appears in the document and then disappears: no projection across the 40.1 million acres of potentially affected environment follows. I ask that the agency apply the cited fragmentation range to the 40.1 million acres before any final rule is issued.

Deer are similarly addressed in the agency's sources and then set aside. The DEIS cites Wyoming research finding roads built for oil extraction may have altered mule deer migration routes and increased their movement speed. The agency's own Tribal record credits the rule's protection with the recovery of deer and moose populations in Alaska by preserving old-growth winter shelter. The DEIS also cites the finding that elk survival rates increased during a road closure and decreased when the gates were removed (Cole 1997), and that elk avoid roads and select unroaded habitat. None of this research is carried forward into a population-level projection. The agency should project the effects on big game populations and hunter opportunity under each alternative, and explain why it has not done so here.

The DEIS cites the estimate that these inventoried roadless areas contain about 5 percent of the stored forest carbon in the coterminous United States, roughly 0.9 billion metric tons. The document then concludes these lands will continue to sequester and store carbon, a conclusion that assumes the rule remains in place, not that it is rescinded. No analysis of what harvest and roading would do to that storage appears anywhere in the proposal. The agency must quantify the projected change in carbon storage and sequestration under each alternative it is considering.

The bear I occasionally see in the Cherokee belongs to a population whose survival depends on unroaded security cover. The DEIS quotes the federal grizzly recovery plan: the increased contact and conflict that come with open roads in grizzly habitat can ultimately end in grizzly mortality, and shooting, habituation and food reward all increase with the use of even secondary unpaved roads. The proposal identifies mitigation for none of it. The agency must disclose, species by species, how the likely adverse effects its own biological assessments identify will be avoided or mitigated, and ESA consultation must be completed and published before any final rule is adopted.

It does not make any financial sense to increase the number of roads that will need to be maintained. The agency is already billions of dollars behind on its existing road maintenance obligations. Building new roads into country that has none compounds a deferred liability the agency has not resolved, and that practical reality reinforces every ecological argument above. I urge the agency to retain the 2001 Roadless Area Conservation Rule without modification.

Sincerely,
Thomas D. Woodbery
Knoxville, TN
